terms.origin: Emerged from decades of AI research; the current usage solidified with the 2023-2024 wave of LLM-based agents.
terms.example: A research agent that searches, reads, and compiles a briefing from one request.
terms.definition: An AI system that takes a goal, breaks it into steps, and carries those steps out using tools, rather than answering a single question and stopping. The defining trait is initiative between instructions: the agent decides what to do next.

terms.example: A support triage agent passing a billing dispute, with full conversation history, to a specialist billing agent.
terms.definition: Transferring control, context, and accumulated state from one agent to another mid-task. Done well, the receiving agent continues without re-asking; done badly, context is lost at the seam and the user repeats themselves.

terms.example: An assistant that remembers your reporting format from last quarter without being retold.
terms.definition: A persistent store that lets an agent recall facts, preferences, and prior work across sessions instead of starting cold each time. Typically split into a short-term working scratchpad and a long-term store, each with different retention and privacy implications.

terms.example: A planner agent assigning research, drafting, and review to three worker agents and assembling the result.
terms.definition: Coordinating multiple agents, tools, and steps toward one goal, including sequencing, retries, and deciding which component handles what. It is the management layer that turns individual capabilities into a working system.

terms.origin: Analyst coinage, popularized by Gartner in 2025 vendor-claim critiques.
terms.example: A vendor rebranding a five-step form automation as "agentic AI" in a sales deck.
terms.definition: Marketing a simple scripted workflow as an autonomous agent to ride the trend. The tell is that the "agent" cannot deviate from its script when conditions change.

terms.origin: Industry usage from roughly 2024 onward, as tool-using LLM systems reached production.
terms.example: A procurement workflow where the AI requests quotes, compares them, and drafts the purchase order.
terms.definition: AI capable of planning and acting autonomously toward a goal, using tools and adjusting course based on results. The term marks the shift from AI that answers to AI that does, which is also the shift that creates most new governance exposure.

terms.example: Invoice intake, extraction, validation, and posting running as one automated sequence.
terms.definition: A coordinated, repeatable process in which AI performs defined steps, usually with fixed order and human checkpoints. Distinct from an agent in that the path is designed in advance rather than chosen at run time.

terms.example: An agent allowed to draft emails freely but required to get approval before sending.
terms.definition: How far an agent may act before a human must confirm, ranging from suggest-only through approve-to-execute to fully autonomous. Setting this level deliberately, per task, is one of the core agent governance decisions.

terms.example: An agent comparing supplier pricing across a dozen vendor portals.
terms.definition: An agent that operates a web browser the way a person does: navigating pages, filling forms, clicking, and extracting data. Powerful for research and procurement tasks, and a new category of access that security reviews often have no slot for.

terms.example: Claude Code fixing a failing test suite and submitting the patch for human review.
terms.definition: An agent that reads a repository, edits files, runs tests, and opens pull requests with limited supervision. It compresses development time and simultaneously raises the question of who reviews machine-written changes.

terms.origin: Introduced as a named capability by Anthropic in October 2024.
terms.example: An agent processing claims inside a legacy desktop application.
terms.definition: An agent capability to operate a graphical interface directly, reading the screen and issuing clicks and keystrokes. It extends automation to software that has no API, which is exactly the software with the fewest guardrails.

terms.origin: Introduced commercially in OpenAI's June 2023 API release; now standard across providers.
terms.example: A model calling a weather API, then a calendar API, to reschedule a site visit.
terms.definition: The mechanism by which a model invokes external tools, APIs, or code through structured requests instead of plain text. It is what connects a language model to real systems, and therefore where read-only assistance becomes action with consequences.

terms.origin: Borrowed from control-systems and human-factors engineering, decades before LLMs.
terms.example: A manager approving each AI-drafted payment before release.
terms.definition: A design that requires human approval at defined checkpoints before an AI action takes effect. The control is only as good as the checkpoint placement: approval fatigue on low-stakes items trains people to rubber-stamp the high-stakes ones.

terms.example: A cap of 25 steps and $5 of inference per task, after which the agent stops and reports.
terms.definition: A hard limit on iterations, time, or spend that stops a runaway agent loop. Agents that retry failed steps can burn unbounded cost pursuing an impossible goal unless something external ends the attempt.

terms.origin: A named research field since the 1990s; revived in LLM form from 2023.
terms.example: A researcher agent, a critic agent, and a writer agent producing a due-diligence memo.
terms.definition: Several specialized agents collaborating, delegating, or debating to solve a task no single agent handles well. The architecture improves quality and adds coordination failure modes that single-agent systems do not have.

terms.example: A lead agent splitting a market analysis into five parallel research threads.
terms.definition: A lead agent decomposes a task and delegates subtasks to subordinate agents, then assembles their outputs. The pattern behind most production "deep research" systems, and the reason one user request can fan out into dozens of model calls.

terms.example: A task graph turning "prepare the board pack" into gather, draft, chart, and review steps.
terms.definition: The component that decomposes a goal into an ordered set of steps before execution begins. Plan quality bounds agent quality: a flawless executor of a bad plan still fails.

terms.example: Extract key figures, then summarize them, then format the summary as an email, as three chained calls.
terms.definition: Connecting prompts in sequence so each step's output feeds the next step's input. The predecessor of full agents, still the right tool when the path is known in advance.

terms.example: A coding agent's plan file listing which modules it intends to touch and why.
terms.definition: A working area where a model writes intermediate reasoning, notes, or plans that inform its final answer but are not the answer. Inspecting it is often the fastest way to see why an agent did what it did.

terms.example: A subagent given read access to one folder to summarize its contents, and nothing else.
terms.definition: A scoped agent spawned to handle one subtask and report back, then terminate. Isolation is the point: the subagent gets only the context and permissions its slice of work requires.

terms.example: A registry granting the finance agent report-generation tools but not payment execution.
terms.definition: The catalog of tools, with their schemas and permissions, that an agent is allowed to call. It is the practical control surface for agent blast radius: an agent cannot misuse a tool it was never granted.

terms.example: Running injection, boundary, and output tests against a customer-facing chatbot before launch.
terms.definition: Deliberately attacking your own AI system to find what breaks before someone else does. It goes beyond functional QA: the tester behaves like an adversary, probing injection paths, boundary conditions, and output handling rather than confirming the happy path works.

terms.example: A grid showing each agent's permitted data sources, write targets, and downstream actions, with every blank cell explained.
terms.definition: The documented limit on what an agent may read, write, and trigger. Writing boundaries down is the control: an undocumented boundary cannot be audited, and in a boundary matrix the empty cells are findings, not omissions.

terms.origin: NIST SP 800-18 Revision 2, which extended system security planning to AI systems.
terms.example: An SSP-style document covering a deployed RAG system's data sources, access controls, and monitoring.
terms.definition: Documentation of an AI system's purpose, controls, and monitoring, in the format NIST SP 800-18r2 defines. It extends the long-standing system security plan discipline to AI, giving assessors one place to see what the system does and how it is protected.

terms.origin: OWASP AI Vulnerability Scoring System project.
terms.example: Ranking a prompt-injection exposure against a model-exfiltration risk to decide which gets fixed first.
terms.definition: An OWASP scoring method for rating the severity of AI-specific vulnerabilities, the AI analog of CVSS for conventional software flaws. Scores are what turn a pile of findings into a sequenced remediation roadmap.

terms.term: Annex I / Annex III (EU AI Act)
terms.origin: EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; deadlines amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus.
terms.example: An AI hiring screener landing in Annex III and inheriting the full high-risk obligation stack.
terms.definition: The two routes into high-risk classification under the EU AI Act: Annex I covers AI embedded in already-regulated products, Annex III lists stand-alone high-risk use cases such as hiring and credit. Which annex applies decides the obligation set and the compliance deadline.

terms.origin: Long-standing security-engineering concept, predating AI.
terms.example: An inventory that adds the chatbot's prompt box and its retrieval store to the classic network and application entries.
terms.definition: Every point where an attacker can attempt to reach or influence a system. AI expands it in kind, not just degree: inference endpoints, prompt channels, retrieval sources, and tool calls are all new entry points the pre-AI threat model never listed.

terms.example: A log entry showing which agent approved a refund, under which delegation, at what time.
terms.definition: A tamper-resistant record of who did what, when, and under what authority. Agent actions belong in it exactly as human actions do; an agent that acts outside the logged record is an agent that cannot be investigated.

terms.origin: Borrowed from site-reliability engineering; applied to AI agents from roughly 2024.
terms.example: Measuring what a hijacked procurement agent could actually order, cancel, or pay before a control intervenes.
terms.definition: How much damage a compromised identity or agent can cause before anything stops it. Read access leaks data; write access changes systems, which is why write permissions are what make a blast radius large.

terms.origin: EU product-conformity regime, extended to AI by the EU AI Act.
terms.example: An AI-enabled medical device carrying a CE mark while still needing its own security assessment.
terms.definition: A manufacturer's declaration that a product meets EU requirements and may be sold in the single market. It is a statement of product compliance, not a security assurance: a CE mark says the conformity process ran, not that the system resists attack.

terms.origin: Standard audit and compliance vocabulary, notably from PCI DSS.
terms.example: A WAF rule blocking a known exploit pattern while the underlying patch waits for a maintenance window.
terms.definition: A substitute control applied when the preferred control cannot be deployed in time. It buys risk reduction now at the cost of tracking debt: every compensating control carries an implicit promise to install the real one.

terms.origin: EU product-safety law; central to the EU AI Act's high-risk regime.
terms.example: A high-risk AI system routed through a notified body instead of a self-declaration.
terms.definition: The formal process of demonstrating a product meets regulatory requirements before it goes to market. Depending on classification it is self-assessed or third-party assessed, and the difference determines cost, timeline, and who signs.

terms.example: A multi-tenant assistant that never lets tenant A's retrieved documents surface in tenant B's answers.
terms.definition: Keeping one user's prompts, retrieved data, and cached results out of another user's session. Failures here are leaks with no attacker involved: the system volunteers one tenant's data to another through shared context or cache.

terms.term: COSAiS (Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems)
terms.origin: NIST Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems project.
terms.example: Selecting the overlay controls for a generative AI deployment instead of hand-picking from 800-53.
terms.definition: A NIST project mapping the SP 800-53 control catalog onto AI systems. It is the implementation detail beneath the Cyber AI Profile: where the profile says what outcomes matter, the overlays say which controls produce them.

terms.origin: NIST IR 8596.
terms.example: Mapping an existing CSF 2.0 program onto AI systems using the profile's Secure, Defend, and Thwart lenses.
terms.definition: A NIST profile applying the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 to AI, organized around securing AI systems, defending with AI, and thwarting AI-enabled attacks. It bridges CSF 2.0 and the AI RMF so security teams do not need two disconnected frameworks.

terms.origin: EU Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847.
terms.example: A software vendor's CRA conformity work counting toward its AI Act cybersecurity obligations.
terms.definition: An EU regulation setting lifecycle cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, from secure development through vulnerability handling and updates. Its Article 12(1) deems CRA compliance to satisfy part of AI Act Article 15, tying the two regimes together.

terms.origin: Established security control category; AI-channel coverage is the current gap.
terms.example: Extending DLP policies to inspect what employees paste into public AI tools.
terms.definition: Controls that detect and block sensitive data leaving the organization. Classic DLP watches email, uploads, and endpoints; it is rarely tuned to watch a prompt box, which is now one of the busiest exfiltration channels in the building.

terms.example: Tracing a fine-tuning dataset back to its licensed sources before a customer audit asks.
terms.definition: A verified record of where data came from and what it may be used for. Consent, licensing, and residency obligations travel with the data into every model that touches it, so provenance is what makes a training set defensible rather than merely available.

terms.example: A signed risk assessment with a date and an owner, produced in response to a regulator's request.
terms.definition: A dated, owned artifact that answers what the organization knew and when it knew it. Assurance is an opinion; evidence is a document, and a regulator or plaintiff accepts only the second.

terms.origin: EU Digital Omnibus package, 2026.
terms.example: Replanning an AI Act compliance roadmap around the deferred Annex III date instead of the original 2026 deadline.
terms.definition: The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment. Its practical effect is calendar relief, not obligation relief: Annex III high-risk duties moved to December 2027 while transparency dates held.

terms.origin: GDPR Article 35.
terms.example: Completing a DPIA before deploying an AI system that screens customer communications.
terms.definition: A documented assessment of privacy risk required before certain high-risk processing. Many AI deployments trigger the duty because they process personal data in new ways at scale, and the DPIA is often the first document a supervisory authority requests.

terms.origin: EU standardisation system under Regulation (EU) 1025/2012.
terms.example: Building an AI quality-management system against the harmonised standard instead of arguing conformity from first principles.
terms.definition: A European standard that, once cited in the Official Journal, gives a presumption of conformity with the regulation it supports. Following the standard becomes the practical route to compliance because it shifts the burden of proof onto anyone claiming otherwise.

terms.origin: Codified in NIST SP 800-61.
terms.example: A tabletop exercise walking the team through a prompt-injection incident before one happens.
terms.definition: The documented and rehearsed process for detecting, containing, and recovering from a security event. The rehearsal is the substance: an untested plan is treated as no plan, because the first live incident is the worst possible rehearsal.

terms.example: An inventory pass that finds five machine credentials for every employee login.
terms.definition: Any credential belonging to software rather than a person: service accounts, API keys, certificates, tokens. They now outnumber human identities in most environments, and each new agent adds several more.

terms.origin: SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules, 2023.
terms.example: A materiality assessment convened within hours of discovering a breach involving an AI system.
terms.definition: Whether an event is significant enough to require disclosure to investors or regulators. For US public companies a materiality determination on a cyber incident starts the SEC's four-business-day disclosure clock, which makes the determination itself a governed process.

terms.origin: MITRE ATLAS, launched 2021.
terms.example: Mapping a deployed model's exposures against ATLAS techniques during a threat-modeling session.
terms.definition: A public knowledge base of observed adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, the ATT&CK equivalent for AI. It turns AI threat modeling from speculation into pattern-matching against documented attacks.

terms.example: Including model weights and adapters in the disaster-recovery inventory with defined restore objectives.
terms.definition: The weights, adapters, and tuning data that constitute a trained model. It is a production asset with recovery requirements: losing it can mean losing a capability no backup of the surrounding code can restore.

terms.example: Rate and pattern monitoring that flags a customer account systematically mapping a model's decision boundary.
terms.definition: Extracting a model's behavior or training data through repeated queries. Each request looks legitimate on its own; the theft only appears in the aggregate pattern, which is why per-request controls miss it.

terms.origin: Federal Reserve SR 26-2 and OCC Bulletin 2026-13, April 2026, superseding SR 11-7.
terms.example: A bank's validation team independently testing an AI credit model before it touches a lending decision.
terms.definition: Supervisory expectations for validating and governing models used in regulated decisions: independent validation, ongoing monitoring, and documented limitations. SR 26-2 and OCC 2026-13 replaced the long-standing SR 11-7 in April 2026, extending the discipline explicitly to AI and machine learning models.

terms.example: A register listing the base model, dataset sources, and pipeline dependencies behind each deployed AI system.
terms.definition: Everything a model depends on that the organization did not build: base weights, tuning datasets, training pipelines, and the services that host them. Each inherited component carries inherited risk that procurement never priced.

terms.origin: NIST SP 800-207, published 2020.
terms.example: Using 800-207 tenets to design per-request authorization for agent tool calls.
terms.definition: The NIST publication defining zero trust architecture and its tenets: verify every request, assume breach, grant least privilege. It was written before agent traffic existed, so applying it to AI means extending its identity and policy model to non-human actors it never anticipated.

terms.example: An access-review cycle that includes agent credentials with the same rigor as user accounts.
terms.definition: Any identity that can authenticate and act without a person present: service accounts, workload identities, and now AI agents. It is the population most access reviews miss, because review processes were designed around employees.

terms.origin: EU conformity-assessment regime; designated per regulation including the AI Act.
terms.example: Booking a notified-body assessment slot months ahead of a high-risk system's market date.
terms.definition: An accredited organization designated to carry out third-party conformity assessment under EU product law. For the AI Act's high-risk systems, notified-body capacity is the current constraint: obligations can arrive faster than assessors can be accredited.

terms.example: A filter redacting account numbers from a support bot's answers regardless of how they entered the context.
terms.definition: Inspecting generated responses before release and blocking or redacting what should not go out. It is the last line: it catches what retrieval pulled in, what the prompt coaxed out, and what upstream controls missed.

terms.origin: OWASP, first released 2023.
terms.example: Structuring an AI application security review as a walk through the ten categories.
terms.definition: The consensus list of the highest-priority security risks in LLM applications, from prompt injection through unbounded consumption. It functions as the scoring baseline for AI application security the way the original OWASP Top 10 does for web.

terms.example: An agent's payment attempt checked against amount and counterparty policy at call time.
terms.definition: Evaluating each attempted action against policy at the moment it is attempted, rather than trusting a role granted in advance. It is enforcement, not documentation: the policy engine sits in the execution path and can say no.

terms.origin: EU product-safety law doctrine.
terms.example: Citing conformity with a harmonised standard as the front-line answer to an enforcement inquiry.
terms.definition: The legal assumption that following a cited standard satisfies the underlying regulatory requirement. It shifts the burden of proof: a challenger must show the standard was not followed or does not cover the case, rather than the deployer proving compliance from scratch.

terms.origin: Differential privacy literature, Dwork et al., 2006.
terms.example: A vendor asked to state the epsilon behind its privacy-preserving analytics claim.
terms.definition: The parameter, epsilon, bounding how much any single record can influence a model's output under differential privacy. The number is the claim: a "differentially private" system quoted without an epsilon value is an unevidenced assertion.

terms.origin: GDPR Article 17.
terms.example: A deletion workflow that removes the source record and the embeddings generated from it.
terms.definition: An individual's right to have their personal data deleted. In AI systems the practical question is where deletion stops: source rows can be removed while derived embeddings and trained weights still carry the influence, and erasure that stops before the embedding store is incomplete by design.

terms.origin: Standardized formats SPDX and CycloneDX; mandated in US federal procurement by EO 14028.
terms.example: Requiring an SBOM from an AI vendor while separately demanding training-data licensing terms.
terms.definition: An inventory of the components and dependencies inside a piece of software. It answers component provenance, not data licensing: an SBOM tells you which libraries shipped, and says nothing about what trained the model beside them.

terms.origin: Cloud identity-platform vocabulary, notably Microsoft Entra.
terms.example: Baselining a service principal's fixed access pattern so deviations alert immediately.
terms.definition: A non-human identity used by an application to authenticate to a service. Its behavior is predictable, which is exactly what distinguishes it from an agent: a service principal does the same thing every night, an agent decides what to do next.

terms.origin: Established security operations category.
terms.example: Routing AI gateway and agent-action logs into the SIEM alongside firewall and endpoint feeds.
terms.definition: The platform that centralizes logs and correlates them into alerts. Its blind spot is whatever never reaches it, and AI gateway logs often never do, leaving the busiest new traffic channel invisible to the team paid to watch.

terms.example: A quarterly release-note review that catches a CRM enabling AI summarization by default.
terms.definition: A vendor switching on an AI feature inside software you already run, with no new contract and no procurement event. It is found in release notes, not purchase orders, which is why AI inventories built from contracts alone undercount what is actually running.

terms.origin: AICPA Trust Services Criteria.
terms.example: Reading a vendor's SOC 2 scope to confirm the AI feature actually sits within the audited boundary.
terms.definition: An attestation report on a service organization's controls over security, availability, and confidentiality, issued by an independent auditor. It is the report enterprise buyers ask for, and its scope section is where AI services quietly fall inside or outside the attestation.

terms.origin: Supply-chain security practice; frameworks include SLSA and Sigstore.
terms.example: Verifying a model file's signature against the publisher's key before loading it into production.
terms.definition: A verified record of where code, containers, and model weights originated, signed and traceable to a source. It is what lets a deployer distinguish the artifact the vendor built from an artifact something substituted along the way.

terms.origin: Established security-engineering practice; methods include STRIDE, from Microsoft.
terms.example: A design review that models prompt injection and retrieval poisoning alongside classic network threats.
terms.definition: Structured analysis of how a system could be attacked, done before it ships. AI adds questions the old model never asked: what can the prompt channel deliver, what can retrieval import, what can a tool call reach.

terms.origin: Institute of Internal Auditors, Three Lines Model, 2020 revision.
terms.example: Assigning AI policy to risk, AI deployment risk to the business, and AI assurance to internal audit.
terms.definition: The IIA framework separating risk ownership (first line), oversight (second line), and independent assurance (third line). AI governance sits in the second line: it sets policy and monitors, while the teams deploying AI own the risk and internal audit independently checks both.

terms.example: A reporting workflow granting read-only tools while the same agent's filing workflow adds one write tool.
terms.definition: Restricting an agent to a defined set of tools evaluated at execution time. Scope it per workflow, not per agent: the same agent doing two jobs should hold two different tool sets, each as small as the job allows.

terms.origin: OWASP LLM Top 10, category LLM10.
terms.example: A spend alert catching an integration retrying a failing model call thousands of times overnight.
terms.definition: Runaway inference volume that imposes cost and exhausts capacity, whether from attack, defect, or an agent loop. It is OWASP LLM10, and in practice it is seen first on an invoice rather than in a dashboard.

terms.origin: Cloud-native identity practice; implementations include SPIFFE and cloud provider workload identity federation.
terms.example: A containerized agent authenticating through its workload identity instead of a shared API key.
terms.definition: An identity assigned to a running workload rather than to a person or an application registration, common in cloud and container platforms. It narrows credentials to the workload's lifetime, which is the right shape for agent processes that spin up and vanish.

terms.origin: Term popularized by Forrester, 2010; codified in NIST SP 800-207, 2020.
terms.example: Applying per-request verification to agent tool calls with the same rigor as user requests.
terms.definition: A security model that verifies every request rather than trusting network location. NIST SP 800-207 defines it, and it is rarely extended to agents: the architecture that never trusts a laptop still routinely trusts whatever an agent asks for once it is inside.

terms.example: ReLU, GELU, and SwiGLU are the common choices in modern models.
terms.definition: A nonlinear function applied to neuron outputs so the network can represent relationships more complex than straight lines. Without nonlinearity, stacking layers adds nothing a single layer could not do.

terms.origin: Introduced in Bahdanau et al., 2014; made central by the 2017 transformer paper.
terms.example: A translation model attending to the right source word regardless of word order.
terms.definition: The component that weights the relevance of each input element when producing each output element, letting a model focus on what matters wherever it sits in the sequence. It is the core of the transformer and the reason context length costs compute.

terms.example: Dimensionality reduction and image denoising pipelines.
terms.definition: A neural network that learns efficient encodings of unlabeled data by compressing it through an encoder and reconstructing it through a decoder. What survives the squeeze is, by construction, the structure the data actually contains.

terms.example: A chat model producing a sentence one token at a time, each chosen in light of the last.
terms.definition: A model that generates each output conditioned on everything it has generated so far. Token-by-token generation is why LLM output streams, and why an early wrong turn can compound through the rest of an answer.

terms.origin: OpenAI, 2021, "Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision."
terms.example: Finding product photos from a text query with no task-specific training.
terms.definition: A model trained to align image and text embeddings in one shared space, so pictures and descriptions of the same thing land near each other. That alignment is what makes zero-shot image classification and text-to-image retrieval work.

terms.origin: LeCun et al., 1989; popularized at scale by AlexNet, 2012.
terms.example: Image classification and defect detection on a production line.
terms.definition: A deep learning architecture that processes visual data by sliding learned filters across an image, detecting edges, textures, and shapes at increasing levels of abstraction. It dominated computer vision for a decade and still runs much of production imaging.

terms.example: A text prompt steering an image diffusion model through cross-attention layers.
terms.definition: Attention where the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another, letting one stream consult a second. It is how a decoder reads an encoder, and how an image generator reads a text prompt.

terms.example: A decoder-only model completing text without a separate encoder stage.
terms.definition: The component that generates output tokens one at a time from a representation and the tokens produced so far. GPT-style chat models are decoder-only: the same stack reads the prompt and writes the answer.

terms.example: Classic transformer LLMs where each forward pass uses the whole network.
terms.definition: A model that activates all of its parameters for every token processed. Simpler to train and serve than sparse alternatives, at the price of spending full compute on every token whether the token needs it or not.

terms.origin: Ho et al., 2020, "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models."
terms.example: Stable Diffusion and Midjourney generating images from text prompts.
terms.definition: A class of generative models that create data by learning to reverse a noising process, iteratively removing noise until an image, video, or audio sample emerges. Quality comes from many small denoising steps rather than one leap.

terms.origin: Peebles and Xie, 2023, "Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers."
terms.example: Video generation models scaling quality by scaling the transformer backbone.
terms.definition: A diffusion model that replaces the U-Net backbone with a transformer, bringing transformer scaling behavior to image and video generation. Most modern large media generators build on this design.

terms.example: BERT-style models embedding sentences for search.
terms.definition: The component that converts input into a dense representation the rest of the system can use. Encoder-only models excel at understanding tasks, classification, retrieval, and similarity, where nothing needs to be generated.

terms.example: T5 translating or summarizing by encoding the source and decoding the target.
terms.definition: An architecture pairing an encoder for the input with a decoder for the output, the natural shape for tasks that transform one sequence into another. Translation and summarization were its home ground before decoder-only models absorbed most tasks.

terms.example: Interpretability work locating factual recall in FFN weights.
terms.definition: The position-wise dense layers inside each transformer block, applied to every token independently between attention steps. Much of what a model knows, its stored factual associations, lives in these layers.

terms.origin: Dao et al., 2022, "FlashAttention."
terms.example: Serving a long-context model at a fraction of the memory cost of naive attention.
terms.definition: A memory-efficient attention implementation that restructures the computation to minimize reads and writes to GPU memory. Same mathematics, dramatically better hardware behavior, which is what made today's long context windows affordable.

terms.origin: Goodfellow et al., 2014.
terms.example: Style transfer, super-resolution, and early deepfake generation.
terms.definition: An architecture in which two networks compete: a generator creates synthetic data and a discriminator judges real from fake, each improving against the other. The adversarial game produced the first convincingly realistic synthetic faces.

terms.example: A RAG system answering from retrieved policy documents and citing them.
terms.definition: Anchoring a model's responses to trusted sources rather than its parametric memory. A grounded answer can cite where it came from; an ungrounded one can only assert.

terms.example: An enterprise graph linking customers, contracts, and obligations for exact traversal.
terms.definition: A connected representation of entities and their relationships, storing facts as a network rather than rows. Paired with LLMs it supplies the precise, multi-hop structure that flat text retrieval loses.

terms.example: GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Claude handling drafting, analysis, and coding tasks.
terms.definition: A generative model trained on vast text corpora, capable of understanding, summarizing, generating, and predicting language. Scale is the operative word: capabilities appear at sizes where the model has absorbed a meaningful fraction of written human knowledge.

terms.example: Morphing between two faces by walking the latent space between them.
terms.definition: The compressed internal representation space where a model organizes what it has learned, with similar concepts sitting close together. Movement through this space is meaningful: interpolating between two points produces coherent blends.

terms.origin: Ba et al., 2016.
terms.example: Pre-norm transformer blocks in most modern LLMs.
terms.definition: A technique that normalizes activations within a layer to stabilize and speed training. Deep networks drift without it; pre-norm placement is one reason very deep transformers train reliably.

terms.example: Reading logits to measure how certain a classifier really was.
terms.definition: The raw, unnormalized scores a model produces before they are converted to probabilities. They are the model's opinion in its most honest form, inspected for confidence and manipulated for steering.

terms.origin: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997.
terms.example: Speech recognition and text generation systems of the pre-transformer era.
terms.definition: A recurrent architecture with gating that lets it retain information across long sequences, solving the vanishing-gradient problem that crippled plain RNNs. It carried speech recognition and translation until transformers displaced it.

terms.origin: Gu and Dao, 2023.
terms.example: Hybrid Mamba-transformer models serving very long documents cheaply.
terms.definition: A selective state space model offering long-context processing with linear time complexity, against attention's quadratic cost. Hybrid designs pair Mamba layers with transformer layers to get length efficiency without giving up attention's strengths.

terms.origin: Anthropic, November 2024; subsequently adopted across the industry.
terms.example: A company exposing its CRM through one MCP server that every AI assistant can call.
terms.definition: An open standard for connecting AI models to tools and data sources through a common interface, so integrations are built once rather than per-model. It is the plumbing standard of the agent era: an MCP server exposes a capability, and any compliant model can use it.

terms.origin: Shazeer et al., 2017, "Outrageously Large Neural Networks."
terms.example: Mixtral routing each token through two of eight experts.
terms.definition: An architecture combining multiple specialized sub-networks with a router that decides which experts process each input. It buys large total capacity at modest per-token compute, since only a few experts fire per token.

terms.origin: Vaswani et al., 2017.
terms.example: Separate heads attending to a pronoun's antecedent and its verb at once.
terms.definition: Running several attention operations in parallel so the model captures different relationship types simultaneously, one head tracking syntax while another tracks reference. Standard in every transformer block.

terms.example: GPT-4o and Gemini analyzing an uploaded diagram and discussing it in text.
terms.definition: Models that process, understand, and generate multiple data types, text, images, audio, video, within one system. The practical effect is that a single interface can read a chart, hear a meeting, and answer in prose. Sometimes shortened to simply multimodal.

terms.origin: McCulloch and Pitts, 1943; modern form via backpropagation, 1986.
terms.example: Feedforward networks underlying all of deep learning.
terms.definition: A computing system inspired by biological neural networks, built from interconnected nodes whose connection strengths are learned from data. Every deep learning system, from image classifiers to LLMs, is a neural network at heart.

terms.origin: Vaswani et al., 2017.
terms.example: Sinusoidal or learned encodings added to token embeddings.
terms.definition: A method for injecting token-order information into a model that otherwise sees an unordered set. Without it, attention cannot distinguish "dog bites man" from "man bites dog."

terms.example: Time-series forecasting and pre-transformer translation systems.
terms.definition: A network class for sequential data in which connections loop, letting past inputs influence present processing. It defined sequence modeling before attention, and its inability to parallelize training is what transformers fixed.

terms.origin: He et al., 2015, "Deep Residual Learning."
terms.example: Standard in every deep architecture since ResNet.
terms.definition: A skip connection that adds a layer's input to its output, giving gradients a direct path through deep networks. It is the structural trick that made networks hundreds of layers deep trainable at all.

terms.origin: Su et al., 2021, "RoFormer."
terms.example: Llama-family models handling contexts longer than trained lengths.
terms.definition: A positional method that rotates query and key vectors by position-dependent angles, encoding relative position directly into attention. It extrapolates to longer sequences better than fixed encodings, which is why most modern open models use it.

terms.example: A router spreading tokens evenly so no expert sits idle while another saturates.
terms.definition: The component in a mixture-of-experts model that selects which experts process each token. Routing quality determines whether capacity is used or wasted, and load balancing across experts is its persistent engineering problem.

terms.origin: Vaswani et al., 2017, "Attention Is All You Need."
terms.example: Resolving what "it" refers to across a long paragraph.
terms.definition: The transformer component that lets every token weigh its relationship to every other token in the sequence, regardless of distance. It is what gives transformers their grasp of long-range context.

terms.example: A query for "reducing churn" surfacing a document titled "customer retention playbook."
terms.definition: Retrieval based on meaning rather than keyword overlap, implemented by comparing embeddings. It finds the document that answers the question even when the question shares no words with it.

terms.example: Phi and Gemma-class models running on a laptop for classification tasks.
terms.definition: A lightweight language model optimized for speed, memory footprint, and edge deployment rather than maximum capability. The trade is deliberate: for bounded tasks, a small model that runs locally beats a frontier model that requires a round trip.

terms.example: Turning logits into the probabilities that sampling draws from.
terms.definition: The function that converts raw scores into a probability distribution summing to one. It is the final step before a model commits to a next-token choice.

terms.example: An MoE model with huge total parameters but modest active compute per token.
terms.definition: A model that activates only a subset of its parameters per token, typically through mixture-of-experts routing. Total capacity grows without proportional inference cost, which is how very large models stay servable.

terms.example: Mamba processing book-length documents at linear cost.
terms.definition: A sequence architecture that maintains a running compressed state, scaling linearly with sequence length where attention scales quadratically. The active alternative to attention for very long inputs.

terms.origin: Vaswani et al., 2017, "Attention Is All You Need."
terms.example: GPT, BERT, Gemini, and Claude are all transformers.
terms.definition: The deep learning architecture built on self-attention, introduced in 2017, that forms the foundation of modern LLMs. Its decisive property was parallelizable training, which let model scale grow with hardware in a way recurrent architectures never could.

terms.origin: Ronneberger et al., 2015.
terms.example: The denoiser inside classic Stable Diffusion.
terms.definition: An encoder-decoder network with skip connections between matching resolution levels, preserving fine detail through the compression bottleneck. Built for medical image segmentation, it became the denoising backbone of the first diffusion image generators.

terms.origin: Kingma and Welling, 2013.
terms.example: The latent compression stage in Stable Diffusion pipelines.
terms.definition: An autoencoder that learns a probabilistic latent distribution rather than fixed codes, making the latent space smooth enough to generate from. In image diffusion systems it handles the compression into and out of latent space.

terms.origin: Dosovitskiy et al., 2020.
terms.example: Image classifiers and the vision encoders inside multimodal models.
terms.definition: An architecture that applies transformer attention to image patches instead of convolutions, treating a picture as a sequence of tiles. At sufficient data scale it matched then passed CNNs, unifying vision and language under one architecture family.

terms.example: CLIP, LLaVA, and GPT-4V-class models describing and reasoning over images.
terms.definition: A multimodal model trained to understand both visual inputs and text, connecting what it sees to what it can say. The bridge that lets a chat model read screenshots, charts, and documents.

terms.origin: American Invitational Mathematics Examination, adopted as an AI benchmark from 2024.
terms.example: A reasoning model reporting its AIME solve rate as a headline capability claim.
terms.definition: A competition mathematics exam repurposed to test advanced multi-step reasoning in models. Its problems resist pattern-matching, which is why reasoning-model releases lead with AIME scores.

terms.origin: Fran\u00e7ois Chollet, "On the Measure of Intelligence," 2019.
terms.example: Models scoring far below humans on puzzles a child solves by inspection.
terms.definition: An abstract reasoning benchmark built from novel visual puzzles that cannot be solved by recalling training data. It is deliberately resistant to memorization, making it one of the few tests that measures generalization rather than recall.

terms.example: Comparing two fraud models without committing to an alert threshold.
terms.definition: The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, a threshold-independent measure of how well a classifier separates classes. It answers "how good is the model overall" before anyone picks an operating point.

terms.example: MMLU scores quoted in every model release announcement.
terms.definition: A standardized test used to compare model performance on a defined task set. Useful for ranking and dangerous for deciding: a benchmark measures the test, and vendors optimize for exactly that.

terms.origin: Papineni et al., 2002.
terms.example: Scoring a translation system against reference translations in a research paper.
terms.definition: An n-gram overlap metric for machine translation quality, scoring how much generated text matches reference translations. A legacy NLP metric: cheap, standardized, and known to reward surface overlap rather than meaning.

terms.origin: Frontier-lab safety evaluation practice.
terms.example: Red-teamers using optimized prompts before certifying a capability absent.
terms.definition: The effort to draw out a model's maximum ability before concluding it cannot do something. It exists to prevent false negatives in safety testing: a model that "cannot" assist with a dangerous task under naive prompting may comply under skilled prompting.

terms.example: Discovering a model's errors concentrate in one costly direction.
terms.definition: A table of true and false positives and negatives that shows exactly how a classifier errs, not just how often. The off-diagonal cells are where the operational story lives.

terms.origin: Arpad Elo's chess rating system, applied to LLMs by LMSYS from 2023.
terms.example: Arena leaderboards ranking chat models by win rate against each other.
terms.definition: A relative skill score derived from pairwise comparisons, imported from chess into model evaluation. It ranks models by human preference in head-to-head matchups rather than absolute test scores.

terms.example: Evaluating an entity-extraction system with one balanced figure.
terms.definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, a single number balancing the two. Standard for classification tasks where both false alarms and misses matter.

terms.origin: Rein et al., 2023, "GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark."
terms.example: Frontier models scored on questions PhDs answer near 70 percent.
terms.definition: Graduate-level science questions designed so that even skilled web search does not yield answers, isolating genuine reasoning from lookup. Its "Google-proof" construction is the point.

terms.example: Subject-matter experts labeling a golden set before an eval run.
terms.definition: The verified correct answer used as the reference for scoring. Every real evaluation needs it, and producing it is usually the expensive part: without trusted ground truth, an eval measures agreement, not accuracy.

terms.origin: Stanford CRFM, 2022.
terms.example: Reading a model's full HELM profile instead of one headline benchmark.
terms.definition: A holistic evaluation framework scoring models across many scenarios and metrics at once, accuracy, robustness, fairness, efficiency, rather than one leaderboard number. Its premise is that no single score describes a model.

terms.example: Pairwise ratings feeding a reward model during alignment training.
terms.definition: Scoring models by having human raters compare outputs and pick the better one. It measures what benchmarks cannot, helpfulness and tone, and inherits every bias of the raters, including a documented preference for confident answers.

terms.origin: OpenAI, 2021, "Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code."
terms.example: Reporting pass@1 on HumanEval in a model card.
terms.definition: A Python coding benchmark scored by unit-test pass rate: the model writes a function, the tests decide. It set the early standard for code capability measurement before larger software-engineering benchmarks arrived.

terms.origin: LMSYS Org, 2023.
terms.example: Checking Arena rankings the week a new model ships.
terms.definition: A crowd-sourced evaluation where users chat with two anonymous models and vote for the better answer, producing an Elo ranking from millions of matchups. The closest thing to a live market price for model quality.

terms.origin: Hendrycks et al., 2020.
terms.example: Model launches quoting MMLU alongside newer, harder benchmarks.
terms.definition: The massive multitask language understanding benchmark: multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects from law to physics. For years the default headline number for model knowledge, now saturating as frontier models cluster near the top.

terms.example: A retrieval check at 200 thousand tokens, with the fact buried mid-document.
terms.definition: A long-context test that plants one fact in a large document and asks the model to retrieve it. It validates that an advertised context window actually functions across its full length and at every depth.

terms.example: A model with modest pass@1 but strong pass@10, usable with retry loops.
terms.definition: The probability that at least one of k sampled attempts is correct, the standard code-generation metric. Pass@1 measures reliability; pass@10 measures whether the capability exists at all.

terms.example: Tracking perplexity on a validation set during pre-training.

see_also.name: Perplexity AI, the answer engine
see_also.note: a search product that shares the name
see_also.label: Not to be confused with

terms.definition: A measure of how well a model predicts a text sample, lower being better. The classic language-modeling quality metric, still used in training but disconnected from downstream usefulness: a lower-perplexity model is not automatically a better assistant.

terms.example: Tuning a compliance monitor toward recall because misses cost more than false alarms.
terms.definition: Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct; recall is the share of true cases found. Every detection system trades one against the other, and the right balance is a business decision, not a modeling one.

terms.example: A nightly suite catching a tone shift after a model version bump.
terms.definition: Rerunning a fixed prompt suite after any change, model version, prompt edit, retrieval update, to detect quality loss. It guards against the silent regressions that provider model updates routinely introduce.

terms.example: Scoring summarizers in research papers before LLM-as-judge methods.
terms.definition: An overlap metric for summarization quality, counting shared n-grams between generated and reference summaries. Like BLEU, a legacy metric: standardized, cheap, and blind to whether the summary is actually faithful.

terms.origin: Jimenez et al., 2023.
terms.example: Coding agents ranked by percentage of real issues resolved.
terms.definition: A software engineering benchmark built from real GitHub issues: the model must produce a patch that passes the repository's own tests. It measures end-to-end engineering, not snippet writing, which made it the defining coding-agent benchmark.

terms.example: A one-page policy naming approved tools and the data classes barred from prompts.
terms.definition: The policy defining permitted and prohibited employee AI use: which tools, which data, which tasks. It is the baseline governance artifact, and an AUP nobody has read governs nothing.

terms.example: Tracking what fraction of code-completion suggestions developers accept.
terms.definition: The share of AI suggestions users actually keep. It is the leading adoption indicator for assistive tools: a falling acceptance rate says the tool is losing the user's trust long before usage numbers drop.

terms.origin: Extension of the FinOps Foundation discipline to AI workloads.
terms.example: A dashboard showing cost per resolved support ticket by model and team.
terms.definition: The discipline of tracking and optimizing AI spend against business value, extending cloud FinOps to inference costs. Its unit is cost per outcome, not cost per token: what matters is what a resolved ticket or drafted contract costs.

terms.origin: EU AI Act Article 4, in force since February 2025.
terms.example: Annual training covering hallucination, data handling, and the approved-tool list.
terms.definition: Baseline workforce understanding of AI capability, limits, and policy: what the tools can do, where they fail, and what the rules are. Under the EU AI Act it is now a legal requirement for providers and deployers, not just good practice.

terms.example: A readiness assessment placing a firm at stage two of five, with a path to three.
terms.definition: A staged framework rating an organization from ad hoc experimentation to an embedded operating model. Its value is diagnostic honesty: knowing which stage you are actually at determines which investments make sense next.

terms.origin: SEC enforcement actions beginning 2024.
terms.example: Enforcement actions against firms claiming AI capabilities they did not have.
terms.definition: Overstating the AI content of a product or company to attract customers or capital. It is now an SEC enforcement target: regulators treat inflated AI claims the same as any other material misstatement.

terms.example: A decision to augment underwriters rather than automate underwriting.
terms.definition: The distinction between AI replacing a task outright and AI increasing a person's output on that task. The line determines role design, headcount planning, and the change-management burden of an initiative.

terms.example: Choosing a vendor contract-review tool over an internal build after pricing the maintenance.
terms.definition: The decision between developing an AI capability in house and licensing a vendor solution. The standard portfolio decision, complicated by AI's pace: what only a custom build could do last year ships as a product feature this year.

terms.origin: From advanced chess, popularized by Garry Kasparov in the late 1990s.
terms.example: An analyst directing AI research sweeps, then making the recommendation personally.
terms.definition: A division of labor where human and AI split work by comparative advantage: machine scale and recall paired with human judgment and accountability. Named for the chess format where human-computer teams beat both grandmasters and engines.

terms.example: A CoE publishing the golden path while product teams build on it.
terms.definition: A central team setting AI standards, tooling, and enablement while business units execute. The hub-and-spoke operating model that balances consistency against speed, and drifts toward bottleneck when the hub tries to do rather than enable.

terms.example: Redesigning review workflows and incentives alongside the tool deployment.
terms.definition: The structured approach to shifting behavior, roles, and incentives during AI rollout. It is the actual constraint on ROI: the technology usually works, and the organization around it usually has not changed enough to capture the value.

terms.origin: Popularized by GitHub Copilot, 2021.
terms.example: A coding copilot completing functions inside the developer's editor.

see_also.name: Microsoft Copilot
see_also.note: Microsoft's assistant, which took the generic name
see_also.label: The product

terms.definition: An AI assistant integrated directly into existing software, suggesting rather than acting autonomously. The dominant enterprise adoption pattern because it upgrades a workflow without replacing it.

terms.example: Choosing an EU-region deployment to keep customer data inside the jurisdiction.
terms.definition: The requirement that data be stored and processed within a specific jurisdiction. It constrains model and provider choice directly: a capability that only runs in another region is a capability the regulated workload cannot use.

terms.example: A support bot resolving six of ten contacts end to end, measured by no-reopen rates.
terms.definition: The share of support contacts fully resolved without a human. The core support-AI metric, and one that punishes gaming: deflection that leaves problems unresolved returns as escalation and churn.

terms.origin: Emerging vendor pricing model, 2024 onward.
terms.example: A vendor quoting per-resolution pricing instead of per-seat subscriptions.
terms.definition: The framing of AI agents as capacity purchased in units of work rather than software seats. It reshapes budgeting and vendor pricing: you buy resolved tickets or processed claims, not licenses.

terms.example: An assistant answering from the firm's own contracts and policies, with citations.
terms.definition: Connecting a model to internal systems of record so its answers reflect company data rather than general knowledge. It is where most enterprise value sits, and most integration cost.

terms.origin: Platform-engineering vocabulary, notably from Spotify.
terms.example: A platform team shipping templates that make the compliant architecture the default.
terms.definition: The approved and supported way to build AI applications internally: sanctioned models, patterns, and guardrails packaged for teams. A good golden path reduces shadow AI more effectively than prohibition, because it makes the sanctioned route the easiest route.

terms.example: A contract pipeline repriced after counting reviewer hours per document.
terms.definition: The labor cost of reviewing and correcting AI output. Heavy review erases ROI: an AI that drafts in seconds but requires senior review in hours may cost more than the process it replaced.

terms.origin: Coined in the 2023 Harvard Business School and BCG field study of consultant AI use.
terms.example: A model acing complex analysis while fumbling a simple formatting request.
terms.definition: The uneven capability boundary where AI excels at some tasks and fails at adjacent, seemingly similar ones. It explains inconsistent user experience and why task-level piloting beats intuition for deciding what to deploy.

terms.example: An audit finding four departments running four overlapping AI subscriptions.
terms.definition: The uncontrolled proliferation of models and AI tools across an organization, each adopted locally and governed nowhere. It drives cost, duplicates spend, and makes a defensible AI inventory impossible until consolidated.

terms.example: A support-AI contract billing per ticket the AI fully resolves.
terms.definition: Charging per resolved task or achieved result instead of per seat or per token. Vendors adopt it where outcomes are countable, support resolutions, qualified leads, and it shifts performance risk from buyer to vendor.

terms.example: An "AI-first" announcement followed by unchanged processes a year later.
terms.definition: Announcing AI initiatives without changing workflows, incentives, or decision rights. Activity without outcomes: the press release ships, the operating model does not, and the value never arrives.

terms.example: Twelve proofs of concept, zero production deployments, two years running.
terms.definition: The condition where AI pilots multiply but none reach production. The dominant enterprise failure mode, usually rooted in pilots designed to demonstrate rather than to integrate.

terms.example: A two-week POC confirming extraction accuracy on real documents.
terms.definition: A small, scoped test validating technical feasibility before larger investment. It answers "can this work," which is a different question from "will this work here," the question the pilot must answer next.

terms.example: Decomposing a paralegal role into twenty tasks and finding eight AI-suitable.
terms.definition: Breaking a job into constituent tasks to identify which are AI-suitable. The basis of honest adoption planning: jobs are rarely automatable, tasks often are, and the split determines the real opportunity.

terms.example: Prioritizing the document-automation project that shows returns within one quarter.
terms.definition: The elapsed time from project start to measurable business benefit. A key portfolio filter: two projects with equal returns are not equal if one pays back in a quarter and the other in two years.

terms.example: A monthly token allocation per team, with alerts at 80 percent.
terms.definition: An allocated spend ceiling on model usage for a team or workload, the FinOps control for AI. Budgets convert open-ended inference cost into a governed resource with an owner.

terms.example: A TCO model where human review and integration dwarf the model bill.
terms.definition: The full lifetime cost of an AI capability: inference, integration, oversight labor, evaluation, and retraining. Routinely understated because the visible API price is the smallest line.

terms.example: Collapsing a five-handoff approval chain once AI handles the assembly steps.
terms.definition: Rebuilding a process around AI capabilities rather than layering AI onto the existing process. It is where the real gains come from: automating a bad process yields a faster bad process.

terms.example: A ZDR clause negotiated before routing client data through a model API.
terms.definition: A vendor commitment not to store prompts or outputs after processing completes. A common enterprise contract term, and one worth verifying against the vendor's actual architecture rather than the sales deck.

terms.example: Gradient descent and decision trees are algorithms; a trained classifier is their output.
terms.definition: A set of step-by-step rules or instructions a computer follows to solve a problem or perform a calculation. In machine learning the algorithm is the recipe for learning from data; the model is what the recipe produces.

terms.example: A monitoring system flagging a login pattern no employee has ever produced.
terms.definition: Identifying data points that deviate materially from expected patterns. It is the workhorse of fraud and intrusion detection precisely because it does not need examples of every attack, only a good model of normal.

terms.origin: Term popularized by Ben Goertzel and Shane Legg, early 2000s.
terms.example: Lab mission statements and policy debates organized around reaching or governing AGI.
terms.definition: Hypothetical AI able to understand, learn, and apply knowledge across any intellectual task at or above human level. The term anchors both investment theses and safety debates, despite no agreed test for when it has arrived.

terms.origin: Term coined by John McCarthy for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.
terms.example: Machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision are all AI subfields.
terms.definition: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions. The umbrella over machine learning, NLP, and everything else in this glossary.

terms.origin: Popularized by Nick Bostrom's "Superintelligence," 2014.
terms.example: The endpoint scenario debated in existential-risk literature.
terms.definition: A hypothetical form of AI far surpassing human intelligence in every field, including creativity, wisdom, and social skill. It matters less as a forecast than as the scenario that motivates much of long-horizon safety research.

terms.example: A meeting tool producing a searchable transcript in real time.
terms.definition: Converting spoken audio into text. Modern ASR approaches human transcription accuracy in clean conditions, which is what made meeting transcription and voice interfaces routine.

terms.origin: Rich Sutton, "The Bitter Lesson," 2019.
terms.example: Choosing a bigger general model over a hand-tuned domain pipeline.
terms.definition: The argument that general methods leveraging computation beat hand-crafted domain knowledge over time, drawn from seventy years of AI history. It is cited to justify betting on scale over feature engineering, and it has aged well.

terms.example: Defect detection on a production line running at camera frame rate.
terms.definition: The field enabling machines to interpret images and video: detecting objects, reading documents, tracking motion. One of the earliest AI capabilities to reach industrial reliability.

terms.example: ImageNet for vision; Common Crawl for language pre-training.
terms.definition: A structured collection of data used to train, evaluate, and test models. Its composition quietly determines what the model can and cannot do, which makes dataset documentation a governance artifact, not housekeeping.

terms.example: A deep network learning edge, texture, and object concepts from pixels alone.
terms.definition: A subset of machine learning based on neural networks with many layers, which learn their own representations from raw data rather than relying on hand-built features. It is the engine behind image recognition, speech, and large language models.

terms.example: Simulating a production-line change on the twin before touching the floor.
terms.definition: A live virtual model of a physical asset or process, fed by real data and used for simulation and optimization. It lets an operator test changes in software before risking them in steel.

terms.example: Spam classification and sentiment analysis running billions of times daily.
terms.definition: Models that classify existing data or predict labels rather than generating new content. The quiet majority of production AI: most deployed models decide, they do not create.

terms.example: Warehouse picking robots handling variable, cluttered objects.
terms.definition: AI operating through a physical body, tied to sensors and actuators, where mistakes have physics. The gap between digital and embodied performance remains one of the field's most stubborn frontiers.

terms.origin: Wei et al., 2022, "Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models."
terms.example: Multi-step arithmetic appearing abruptly as model size crossed a threshold.
terms.definition: A skill that appears only above a certain model scale and was absent in smaller versions. Emergence is why capability forecasting is hard: the next scale step may unlock abilities nobody planned for.

terms.origin: Dominant AI paradigm of the 1970s and 1980s.
terms.example: MYCIN recommending antibiotics from encoded clinical rules in the 1970s.
terms.definition: Early AI that encoded human expert rules into if-then logic for a narrow domain. Its rise and stall carry the field's founding lesson: hand-written rules do not scale to the messiness of the real world.

terms.origin: Google, 2016.
terms.example: Phone keyboards improving prediction from usage that never leaves the device.
terms.definition: Training a shared model across decentralized devices without moving raw data to a central server; only model updates travel. It trades engineering complexity for privacy and residency advantages.

terms.origin: Term coined by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, 2021.
terms.example: GPT, Claude, and Llama serving as bases for countless products.
terms.definition: A large model trained on broad data at scale that serves as the base for many downstream tasks. The economic point is amortization: one enormous training run, adapted cheaply a thousand ways.

terms.example: A new flagship release undergoing pre-deployment safety evaluation.
terms.definition: A model at or near the current maximum of capability, typically the largest and most recently released systems. The designation carries regulatory weight: frontier status increasingly triggers evaluation and reporting obligations.

terms.example: ChatGPT, Midjourney, and Claude producing drafts, images, and code on request.
terms.definition: Models that create new content, text, images, video, audio, code, from patterns learned in training data. The 2022 shift from AI that classifies to AI that produces is what put this glossary on your reading list.

terms.origin: Term coined by Arthur Samuel, 1959.
terms.example: A recommendation engine improving as it observes more behavior.
terms.definition: The subset of AI focused on systems that learn from data and improve with experience rather than following explicitly programmed rules. Nearly everything called AI in production is machine learning underneath.

terms.origin: Hans Moravec, "Mind Children," 1988.
terms.example: Superhuman chess coexisting with clumsy robot manipulation.
terms.definition: The observation that abstract reasoning is comparatively easy for machines while sensorimotor skills that feel effortless to humans are hard. It explains why chess fell decades before laundry folding.

terms.example: Spam filters, chess engines, and voice assistants each excelling at one thing.
terms.definition: AI designed and trained for a specific task or narrow range of tasks, with no ability to generalize beyond it. Every deployed system today is narrow AI, however broad its marketing.

terms.example: Automated earnings summaries generated from financial data.
terms.definition: The subfield focused on producing fluent, human-readable text from data or intent. Once template-driven and stilted, now indistinguishable from drafting, which changed both its usefulness and its risks.

terms.example: Sentiment analysis, translation, and summarization as classic NLP tasks.
terms.definition: The field covering machine understanding and generation of human language. Its problems, translation, sentiment, summarization, were separate research tracks until large language models absorbed most of them into one capability.

terms.example: Intent classification routing tickets in a support system.
terms.definition: The subfield focused on extracting meaning and intent from text, as opposed to producing it. It is what turns "I can't log in" into an actionable support category.

terms.example: Neural document extraction feeding a deterministic rules engine for compliance decisions.
terms.definition: A hybrid approach combining neural networks with symbolic logic and rules: perception from the network, guarantees from the rules. Attractive wherever answers must be both learned and provably compliant.

terms.example: Digitizing invoices before an extraction model reads them.
terms.definition: Extracting machine-readable text from images or scanned documents. Decades old, newly relevant: OCR is the front door through which paper enters every AI document pipeline.

terms.example: Churn and demand forecasting driving retention and inventory decisions.
terms.definition: AI that forecasts outcomes from historical data rather than generating content. It ran the enterprise quietly for a decade before generative AI took the spotlight, and it still makes most of the money.

terms.origin: Class established by OpenAI's o1, September 2024.
terms.example: A reasoning model taking thirty seconds on a proof a chat model fumbles instantly.
terms.definition: A model optimized to work through multi-step problems before answering, spending extra inference compute on deliberate chains of reasoning. The design trade is latency and cost for accuracy on hard problems.

terms.example: Streaming and e-commerce suggestions driving a large share of consumption.
terms.definition: A model that ranks and suggests items based on user behavior and item features. The most economically consequential AI most people touch daily without naming it.

terms.example: Game-playing agents, robotics, and the RL stage of modern model training.
terms.definition: A paradigm in which an agent learns by taking actions in an environment and receiving rewards or penalties, improving through trial and error rather than labeled examples. It trained game champions first and now post-trains reasoning models.

terms.origin: Kaplan et al., 2020; refined by the Chinchilla paper, 2022.
terms.example: Sizing a training run from the curves before committing the budget.
terms.definition: Empirical relationships showing predictable capability gains as compute, data, and parameters increase. They turned model development from craft into capital planning: labs buy capability on a curve.

terms.example: Next-token prediction over trillions of words, no annotators required.
terms.definition: Training in which the model creates its own labels from the data, such as predicting the next token or a masked word. It unlocked web-scale training by removing the human labeling bottleneck, and it is how LLMs are pre-trained.

terms.example: Labeling one percent of records and propagating structure to the rest.
terms.definition: Training on a small labeled set combined with a large unlabeled set, letting scarce annotation stretch across abundant data. The practical middle path when labels are expensive and data is not.

terms.example: Spam-or-not-spam classification learned from labeled email.
terms.definition: Training on labeled input-output pairs so the model learns to predict the label for new inputs. The classic paradigm behind most production classifiers and forecasters.

terms.example: Expert systems of the 1980s encoding knowledge as rules.
terms.definition: Rule-based AI that manipulates explicit symbols and logic rather than learning statistical patterns. The field's first paradigm, and the source of properties neural methods still lack: transparency and guarantees.

terms.example: Audiobook narration generated at production quality.
terms.definition: Converting text into synthetic spoken audio. Modern TTS crossed the naturalness threshold where listeners stop noticing, which enabled voice assistants and also voice-cloning fraud.

terms.example: Fine-tuning a general image model for defect detection with a few thousand examples.
terms.definition: Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for another, carrying learned representations across. It is why a modest dataset can now produce a strong specialized model: most of the learning happened before you arrived.

terms.origin: Alan Turing, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," 1950.
terms.example: Chatbots passing short conversational judgments that Turing proposed in 1950.
terms.definition: A test of whether a machine's conversational behavior is indistinguishable from a human's. Historically the field's north star, now largely superseded: modern models pass casual versions while the interesting capability questions have moved elsewhere.

terms.example: Customer segmentation discovered through clustering rather than assumption.
terms.definition: Learning structure from unlabeled data: clusters, patterns, and groupings no one specified in advance. It finds the categories; humans decide what they mean.

terms.example: Video models that simulate plausible physics when generating motion.
terms.definition: An internal learned representation of how an environment behaves, supporting prediction and planning. Whether large models form genuine world models or surface statistics is one of the field's live arguments.

terms.example: A translation system tracking five candidate renderings before choosing.
terms.definition: A decoding strategy that keeps several candidate sequences alive and expands the most promising, rather than committing to one token at a time. Common in translation, where the best sentence is not always built from the best next word.

terms.origin: Wei et al., 2022, "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning."
terms.example: Adding "think step by step" and watching arithmetic accuracy jump.
terms.definition: A prompting technique that encourages the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. Making the reasoning explicit improves accuracy on multi-step problems and gives reviewers something to inspect when the answer is wrong.

terms.example: A research assistant footnoting each claim to a retrieved document.
terms.definition: Linking generated claims back to the source documents that support them. Required in regulated reporting and increasingly expected everywhere: an answer that cites can be checked, an answer that does not must be trusted.

terms.example: Function arguments generated under a JSON grammar that cannot produce invalid syntax.
terms.definition: Restricting token choices at generation time so output must satisfy a grammar or schema. It converts "usually valid" into "guaranteed valid," which is the difference between a demo and an integration.

terms.example: A long session drifting off format until a fresh thread restores it.
terms.definition: Quality decay as a conversation or working context grows long and noisy: the model starts missing instructions it followed an hour ago. Fixed by summarizing state and restarting clean rather than pushing on.

terms.example: Pasting nine documents when the two relevant ones would score higher.
terms.definition: Filling the context window with as much reference material as possible on the theory that more is better. It often degrades precision: relevance beats volume, and retrieval that selects usually outperforms context that hoards.

terms.example: A 200 thousand token window holding an entire contract set for review.
terms.definition: The maximum number of tokens a model can process and retain during a single interaction: its working memory. Everything the model should consider, instructions, documents, history, must fit inside it.

terms.example: Wrapping a pasted email in tags so its text is analyzed, not obeyed.
terms.definition: Markers that separate instructions from data inside a prompt, XML tags, triple backticks, headers. They reduce the chance the model treats quoted content as commands, which is also the first cheap defense against injection.

terms.origin: Established as a capability in the GPT-3 paper, Brown et al., 2020.
terms.example: Two labeled examples teaching a classification the instructions alone missed.
terms.definition: Providing a few in-context examples that demonstrate the desired output format or task handling. The examples do the teaching: format, tone, and edge-case handling transfer from demonstration better than from description.

terms.example: Raising the penalty to stop a model repeating the same sentence stem.
