terms.definition: AI ROI equals total AI benefit minus total AI cost, divided by total AI cost, expressed as a percentage, with a complete cost denominator covering every real expense the investment generated, not just the subscription fee. It converts cycle-time, capacity, error-rate, and rework measurements into a single figure defensible under financial scrutiny.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: The AI Efficiency Scorecard feeding the same quarterly cadence as the governance review.
terms.definition: The integrated operating discipline that connects business enablement, readiness assessment, risk governance, and security into one management system, installed progressively across the nine books of The Operating Discipline for AI Library. Each book's frameworks sit inside it rather than standing alone.

terms.example: Draft time falling 60% while document turnaround stays at four days.
terms.definition: The elapsed time from the start of a unit of work to its usable completion, the first metric AI efficiency claims must survive. AI that speeds a task while lengthening the full cycle through review and rework has improved nothing measurable.

terms.example: Fewer typos, more confidently wrong figures.
terms.definition: The share of outputs containing defects requiring correction, measured at the workflow level rather than the tool level. AI shifts where errors occur more often than it removes them.

terms.example: An invoice bot handling 70% of volume while the exception queue absorbs two analysts.
terms.definition: The routing of cases that fall outside an automated or AI-assisted path to human judgment. Exception volume is the honest measure of how much a process is actually automated.

terms.example: Value-stream mapping before an AI rollout removing three approval steps no one could justify.
terms.definition: The waste-elimination discipline from manufacturing, applied to AI operations: AI adds capacity, Lean asks whether the underlying process deserved automating at all. Automating a wasteful process produces faster waste.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Risk & Governance Review, Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A chatbot drafting marketing copy classed Low while the same model screening loan applicants is Critical.
terms.definition: A four-tier impact classification for AI-influenced decisions, running Low, Moderate, High, Critical, where each tier prescribes a specific human-oversight control profile: which of the AI Decision Accountability Framework™'s three controls are required and what is added at the higher tiers. Classification is by the decision's impact, not the tool's sophistication.

terms.origin: Introduced in Volume I and extended in Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library, by Stephen R. Jordan.
terms.example: A credit denial traceable to a named reviewer, not a model version.
terms.definition: The upstream control framework assigning a named human owner to every consequential AI-influenced decision, with three core controls the Decision Influence Matrix™ scales by impact tier. It exists so that "the AI decided" is never the answer to a board, regulator, acquirer, or plaintiff.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Risk & Governance Review, Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A silent model drift caught by output monitoring and triaged before customer harm.
terms.definition: The framework defining what counts as an AI incident, who responds, and in what order: detection, containment, root-cause, notification, and corrective action, wired to regulatory clocks like the EU AI Act's serious-incident reporting. AI incidents differ from IT incidents because the system keeps producing confident output while wrong.

terms.origin: Introduced in Volume I and extended in Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library, by Stephen R. Jordan.
terms.example: A high-scoring use case pulled into quarterly management review while low scores run on spot checks.
terms.definition: The scoring instrument run against each AI use case across the AI Operational Risk Categories™, producing the risk profile that drives oversight intensity, review cadence, and sign-off requirements.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Risk & Governance Review, Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A one-page executive summary opening the quarterly package.
terms.definition: The recurring eight-section board artifact supporting the oversight mandate: a structured summary, executive summary first, with drill-down detail accessible rather than attached. Built so directors can evidence Caremark-grade oversight of AI.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Risk & Governance Review, Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A firm scoring 11 setting a twelve-month target of 18.
terms.definition: A company-wide scoring instrument rating governance maturity across five dimensions, oversight, accountability, controls, documentation, and review cadence, each on a five-point scale from Ad Hoc to Optimized, summing to a Governance Maturity Index of 5 to 25.

terms.origin: Introduced in Volume I and extended in Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library, by Stephen R. Jordan.
terms.example: An employee's new-tool request routed through the policy's approval path instead of a Slack thread.
terms.definition: The always-on policy governing which AI tools and uses are approved, under what conditions, and through what request path, replacing case-by-case improvisation with a standing rule set.

terms.example: A data science team validating its own model, collapsing three lines into one.
terms.definition: The governance model separating operational ownership (first line), risk and compliance oversight (second line), and independent internal audit (third line), now applied to AI systems. AI blurs the model because the same team often builds, uses, and checks the model, which is exactly the condition the three lines exist to prevent.

terms.example: Shadow AI use entering the register with an owner and a remediation date.
terms.definition: The living inventory of identified risks with owner, severity, likelihood, and treatment, which AI governance frameworks extend with AI-specific entries. An unregistered AI risk is unmanaged by definition.

terms.origin: Federal Reserve SR Letter 11-7, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, 2011.
terms.example: An LLM-based underwriting assistant swept into the model inventory under SR 11-7.
terms.definition: The Federal Reserve's 2011 supervisory guidance on model risk management, the de facto ancestor of AI governance: model inventory, independent validation, and effective challenge. Bank examiners now read AI systems through its lens, whether or not the institution calls them models.

terms.origin: Formalized as clause 9.3 of ISO/IEC 42001:2023.
terms.example: A quarterly review adjusting audit cadence after two AI incidents.
terms.definition: The recurring leadership evaluation of the governance system itself, required by ISO/IEC 42001 clause 9.3: whether the system is adequate, effective, and resourced. The minutes are the audit evidence that oversight actually happened.

terms.origin: In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation, Delaware Court of Chancery, 1996.
terms.example: Board minutes documenting recurring AI risk reporting as Caremark evidence.
terms.definition: The Delaware doctrine that boards must implement and monitor a reporting system for mission-critical risks, with personal liability for conscious failure to oversee. AI's arrival on the mission-critical list makes it the legal floor under board AI oversight.

terms.origin: Article 72 of the EU AI Act.
terms.example: Field performance data triggering a model update and a refreshed conformity assessment.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act obligation to monitor a high-risk AI system's performance after deployment and feed findings back into the risk-management system. Deployment is where the obligation starts, not where it ends.

terms.example: A two-hour exercise revealing nobody knew who could shut the chatbot off.
terms.definition: A facilitated walkthrough of a simulated incident testing whether response plans, roles, and escalation paths actually work before a real event does. AI tabletops rehearse scenarios like silent drift, prompt injection, or an unannounced vendor model change.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A use case scoring high on adoption but failing data reliability, capping its index.
terms.definition: The scoring mechanism of the AI Readiness & Performance Assessment™: six diagnostic scores rolling into a cumulative readiness index that drives the expand, refine, or pause decision. Readiness is scored, not felt.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: Rising copilot logins against flat cycle times failing the test.
terms.definition: The diagnostic module determining whether AI is producing measurable business results or merely activity that looks productive. Not a vendor dashboard review or utilization report, a financial and operational control test asking one question: what changed in the business after AI entered.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: Three people in the same role using three different unapproved tools three different ways.
terms.definition: The diagnostic module evaluating how employees actually use AI, by behavior rather than license counts, logins, or enthusiasm: who uses it, with which tools, approved or not, consistently across roles or not, reviewed before use or not.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: An approval queue that doubled after an AI drafting tool arrived.
terms.definition: The diagnostic module locating where AI-supported workflows create rework, bottlenecks, workarounds, double-handling, approval delays, or hidden administrative loops. Its question: where is AI creating work the business is not officially measuring.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A quoting process with three unofficial variants failing review before any AI touches it.
terms.definition: The diagnostic module asking whether a process is clear enough for AI to support it reliably. A workflow nobody can describe consistently is not ready for automation, whatever the tool demo suggests.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A matrix row exposing a revenue-critical use case with no named owner.
terms.definition: The diagnostic module evaluating leadership accountability: does every meaningful AI use case have a named owner, review authority, escalation discipline, and executive oversight.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: Expansion halted on a failed data-reliability condition with a 60-day reassessment.
terms.definition: The formal decision record stopping a use case's expansion until its foundation is repaired: the suppression trigger, the failed readiness condition, the business consequence of continuing, corrective actions, repair owner, and reassessment date. A pause from assessment defends better than a pause forced by visible failure.

terms.term: Expand, Refine, or Pause Decision Protocol™
terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A strong index overridden by a suppression rule, forcing refine before expand.
terms.definition: The executive decision module converting the assessment into action: six diagnostic scores, the cumulative readiness index, and critical suppression rules determining each use case's next step. A governance control, not a strategy slogan.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Business Enablement Audit, Volume I of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A quarterly AI performance review run on baselines, not anecdotes.
terms.definition: The discipline of measuring AI's business performance with the same rigor as financial performance once meaningful spending, operational reliance, and decision-making attach to AI systems. Perception that work "feels faster" is not measurement, and impressions will not justify continued investment.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Business Enablement Audit, Volume I of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A two-hour synthesis session completing all four for a 40-person firm.
terms.definition: The four artifacts the AI Business Enablement Audit™ produces: the AI inventory, the cost and performance baseline, the risk map, and the governance gap list. Together they are the factual foundation every later volume builds on.

terms.example: A firm inventorying twelve use cases across four departments.
terms.definition: A specific, bounded application of AI to a defined business task with an identifiable owner, input, and output, the unit at which AI is governed, measured, and approved. "We use ChatGPT" is not a use case; "AI drafts first-pass proposal responses, reviewed by the proposals lead" is.

terms.example: A four-day proposal turnaround recorded before the AI rollout, cited after it.
terms.definition: The documented pre-AI measurement of a metric, cycle time, error rate, cost, capacity, against which any AI improvement claim is tested. No baseline, no provable improvement, only impressions.

terms.example: A readiness assessment gating an expansion the leadership team was ready to approve on instinct.
terms.definition: The demonstrated condition of a business being able to absorb AI productively: clear workflows, reliable data, real adoption, governance ownership, and measurable performance, established by assessment rather than asserted by enthusiasm.

terms.example: A pricing use case paused because three spreadsheets disagreed on the current rates.
terms.definition: Whether the information an AI use case relies on is reliable enough for the task: accurate, current, consistent, and owned. It requires practical internal controls, not a data science team or enterprise warehouse.

terms.example: A quarterly attestation that the model inventory is complete and current.
terms.definition: A signed, dated assertion by a named person that a control was performed or a condition holds, converting governance from claimed to evidenced. AI governance runs on attestations because auditors and regulators accept signatures, not vibes.

terms.origin: CEN-CENELEC, Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes, approved July 12, 2026.
terms.example: An ISO 42001-certified provider gap-assessing its management system against EN 18286 ahead of conformity assessment.
terms.definition: The first European standard written specifically to operationalize the EU AI Act: a quality management system standard for providers of high-risk AI systems, mapping directly onto Article 17 and structured around the AI system rather than the organization-centric template of ISO 9001 and ISO/IEC 42001, with mapping annexes back to both. Published by CEN-CENELEC, its Official Journal citation, the step that confers a presumption of conformity under Article 40, is still pending.

terms.origin: Adopted by the European Parliament June 16 and the Council June 29, 2026; signed July 8, 2026.
terms.example: A compliance team re-baselining its high-risk roadmap to December 2027 while keeping Article 50 on the original clock.
terms.definition: The 2026 EU amending regulation that deferred the AI Act's high-risk obligations, Annex III standalone systems to December 2, 2027 and Annex I embedded systems to August 2, 2028, while leaving Article 50 transparency at August 2, 2026 and adding a new Article 5 prohibition on AI-generated child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate imagery. A deferral of the heaviest lift, not a dismantling: registration duties and the Act's architecture stand.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: A proposal team whose NEYR™ fell after an AI drafting tool, because review and correction hours rose faster than drafting time dropped.
terms.definition: The performance ratio measuring whether AI is producing more usable business value per unit of labor, calculated as net completed output value divided by total labor hours across generation, review, correction, and release. A rising NEYR™ means AI is producing more usable value per labor hour; a flat NEYR™ means AI activity is not changing the economics of the workflow; a declining NEYR™ means AI may be creating correction debt or rework that exceeds the visible time savings. Its discipline: do not scale what you cannot measure.

terms.origin: Coined by Stephen R. Jordan in The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, Volume II of The Operating Discipline for AI Library.
terms.example: An OLF™ climbing as employees quietly build spreadsheet workarounds around an AI tool nobody trusts.
terms.definition: The friction ratio that turns a vague "AI is creating more work" complaint into a measurable control indicator, calculated as total weekly untracked manual correction, verification, reformatting, and bypass hours divided by total weekly AI-supported workflow volume. A rising OLF™ means the workflow is creating more hidden administrative drag per unit of output; a flat OLF™ means friction is not improving despite continued use; a declining OLF™ means corrective action may be working and the workflow moving toward readiness.

terms.origin: Colorado SB 24-205 (2024), repealed by SB 26-189, 14 May 2026.
terms.example: A vendor questionnaire still asking for Colorado AI Act compliance a year after the repeal.
terms.definition: The Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act, SB 24-205, which would have been the first comprehensive US state AI law, repealed by SB 26-189 on 14 May 2026 before it ever took effect. It is still widely cited as a live model other states are copying, which is the most common error in US state AI briefings. The Colorado Privacy Act's profiling opt-out survived the repeal untouched and is what actually binds there today.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 22.
terms.example: An automated credit refusal triggering a right to human intervention and an explanation.
terms.definition: The GDPR provision giving people the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal or similarly significant effects. It predates the EU AI Act by eight years, is fully enforced now, and reaches automated decisions whose AI Act obligations have been deferred to 2027 and 2028.

terms.origin: Organizational practice; not a statutory role under the EU AI Act.
terms.example: An AI Officer signing off on the risk classification of every new AI deployment.
terms.definition: The named executive accountable for AI risk across an organization, translating between leadership, legal, and technical teams. Unlike the Data Protection Officer under GDPR, the role is not created by statute, so its authority comes entirely from how the organization defines it. An AI Officer without budget or veto is a title, not a control.

terms.origin: Organizational practice; not a statutory role.
terms.example: A coordinator keeping the AI register accurate so the officer's decisions rest on real data.
terms.definition: The operational counterpart to the AI Officer, running day-to-day governance: maintaining the AI inventory, chasing documentation, scheduling reviews, and keeping records current. The role exists because governance fails at the administrative layer far more often than at the decision layer.

terms.origin: Advisory market practice, following the fractional CFO and virtual CISO models.
terms.example: A 200-person manufacturer retaining a fractional AI Officer two days a month to chair its AI review board.
terms.definition: A part-time or shared AI Officer engaged by organizations that need accountable AI governance but cannot justify a full-time executive. The accountability is identical to the in-house role, only the headcount differs. For most mid-market operators this is the realistic form the role takes.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Articles 37 to 39.
terms.example: A DPO advising on a DPIA while an AI Officer owns the AI Act obligations.
terms.definition: The independent privacy role GDPR requires where an organization's core activities involve large-scale systematic monitoring or large-scale special-category processing. The DPO reports to the highest level of management and cannot be penalised for doing the job. The role is frequently, and wrongly, assumed to cover AI governance. Note the acronym collision: in machine learning, DPO means Direct Preference Optimization.

terms.origin: Adapted from model risk management practice, notably SR 11-7 and its 2026 successor.
terms.example: The head of talent acquisition listed as model owner for the CV screening tool.
terms.definition: The named individual accountable for one specific AI system across its life: purpose, performance, documentation, and failures. When the system misbehaves, the owner gets the call. Every entry in the AI register needs one, and the vendor is not an acceptable answer.

terms.origin: Control-systems and human-factors engineering, adopted into AI governance vocabulary.
terms.example: An analyst watching an automated pricing engine, able to halt it before the next cycle.
terms.definition: A design where AI executes autonomously while a human monitors and retains the power to intervene mid-run. It suits medium-risk, reversible decisions where approving every step would destroy the value of automating it. The control only works if the monitor can see what the system is doing in time to stop it.

terms.origin: Control-systems and human-factors engineering; the third rung of the oversight ladder.
terms.example: An AI system auto-tagging support tickets, with a weekly sample review.
terms.definition: A design where AI acts alone and humans review after the fact, if at all. Defensible only for low-risk, easily reversible actions with reliable logging, because the audit trail is the sole remaining control. Most organizations arrive here by drift rather than by decision.

terms.origin: Human-factors research from the 1990s onward; named in EU AI Act Article 14(4)(b).
terms.example: A reviewer approving an AI recommendation they would have questioned from a colleague.
terms.definition: The documented tendency of people to over-trust automated output and under-apply their own judgment, which strengthens the more fluent and confident the system's explanation sounds. The EU AI Act names it explicitly: human oversight measures for high-risk systems must keep operators aware of it. It is the mechanism by which human-in-the-loop quietly becomes rubber-stamp.

terms.origin: Descriptive governance term rather than a term of art; the observed failure mode of human-in-the-loop controls.
terms.example: A queue of 400 daily AI recommendations cleared at a rate no one could genuinely review.
terms.definition: The failure mode where a human approver signs off on AI output without real scrutiny, producing the paperwork of governance without the substance. It passes an audit that counts approvals and fails one that tests them. Approval fatigue on low-stakes items is the usual cause.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 6 to 27; deadlines amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus.
terms.example: A CV screening tool inheriting the whole high-risk stack because hiring is an Annex III use case.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act tier carrying the full obligation stack: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy and robustness, and conformity assessment. Systems arrive either as safety components of already-regulated products (Annex I) or through the listed use cases in Annex III, such as hiring, credit, education, and essential services. The 2026 Digital Omnibus deferred these duties to December 2027 and August 2028; it did not defer the strict product liability that attaches to failing them.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 50.
terms.example: A customer service chatbot disclosing that it is an AI system at the start of the conversation.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act tier where the duty is disclosure rather than documentation: people must be told they are interacting with AI, and synthetic content must be marked as such. It covers chatbots, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, and deepfakes. Its deadline of 2 August 2026 was left untouched by the Digital Omnibus, so it now lands well before the high-risk obligations it was originally scheduled behind.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 5; extended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus.
terms.example: An employer dropping a sentiment-detection feature that scored staff mood during calls.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act's banned uses, applicable since 2 February 2025 and carrying the highest penalties, up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent of global turnover. They include social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, exploitation of vulnerability, and most real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces. The 2026 Digital Omnibus added AI-generated child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate imagery.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(63) and Chapter V.
terms.example: A company building on a frontier model inheriting the provider's documentation rather than producing its own.
terms.definition: A model trained on broad data that can perform a wide range of distinct tasks and be built into many downstream systems. The EU AI Act gives GPAI providers their own obligation set, technical documentation, information for downstream providers, a copyright policy, and a public summary of training content, applicable since 2 August 2025. Most of the burden sits with the model provider rather than the business deploying it, which is the point deployers most often get wrong in both directions.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 51.
terms.example: A frontier lab running adversarial evaluations and reporting incidents to the AI Office.
terms.definition: The EU AI Act's heavier tier for general-purpose models capable of significant impact at scale, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds ten to the twenty-fifth floating-point operations. It adds model evaluation, adversarial testing, serious-incident reporting, and cybersecurity duties on top of the standard GPAI set. Only a small number of models are in scope, and essentially none are trained by the businesses deploying AI.

terms.origin: Practitioner and vendor coinage; no standing in the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, or the NIST AI RMF.
terms.example: A system record that lapses annually unless the owner re-validates its risk assessment.
terms.definition: A vendor and practitioner term for a per-system governance record covering purpose, owner, data, risk tier, and review status, sometimes with an expiry that forces re-validation. It is not regulatory terminology; the standard equivalents are the AI inventory and the AI system register. The expiry idea is the useful part, treating authority to operate as time-limited rather than permanent.

terms.origin: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 27.
terms.example: A bank documenting affected groups and mitigation before switching on an AI credit model.
terms.definition: The pre-deployment assessment the EU AI Act requires from certain deployers of high-risk systems, covering who could be affected, how, and what mitigation and oversight will be in place. It falls on public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers using AI for credit scoring or life and health insurance pricing. It is a deployer duty, distinct from the provider's conformity assessment and from the GDPR's DPIA, though the three are routinely conflated.

terms.origin: Governance practice; underpins the evidence expectations in ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act's oversight duties.
terms.example: An entry showing the risk lead accepted an AI recommendation, with the reasoning and the date.
terms.definition: The record of who approved which AI-influenced decision, when, and on what reasoning. Distinct from system logs: it captures the human judgment rather than the machine trace, and it is the artifact that answers who decided this when a regulator, an auditor, or a claimant asks. Named humans, timestamps, and rationale, not just code output.

terms.origin: Governance practice; serious-incident reporting duty at Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 73.
terms.example: A near-miss logged when an AI-drafted client email was caught before sending.
terms.definition: The running log of AI failures, near-misses, and complaints, with cause, impact, and remediation. The near-misses are the point: they are the only cheap warning an organization gets. The EU AI Act separately requires providers of high-risk systems to report serious incidents to authorities, and a register is what makes reporting on a deadline possible.

terms.example: An organisation adopting a third-party scheduling agent from a vendor catalogue without a supplier assessment covering what data it may reach.
terms.definition: A venue where agents, tools, or agent capabilities are published, discovered, and consumed by other parties, sometimes with payment and contractual terms attached. Marketplaces move agents squarely into third-party risk: the operator inherits the behaviour of code it did not write, under terms it may not have read, while the assessment categories for this class of supplier are still forming.

terms.example: Dozens of agents independently searching a codebase for a defect, with attention converging on the files several of them flag.
terms.definition: A multi-agent pattern where many simple, largely interchangeable agents work the same problem in parallel with little central control, and the useful result emerges from their interaction rather than from any one agent's plan. It differs from an orchestrated multi-agent system, where a leader assigns roles, and it is harder to govern for the same reason: there is no single place where the decision was made and no single log that explains it.

terms.example: A planning agent delegating a purchase step to a procurement agent that holds the spending limit, rather than passing the limit along with the task.
terms.definition: The transfer of a task, and the authority to act on it, from a person or one agent to another. Delegation differs from a handoff because it carries permission: the receiving agent may spend, call tools, or commit on the delegator's behalf. The governing question is therefore not what was passed but what authority went with it, whether that authority narrows at each hop, and whether it can be revoked while a run is still in flight.

terms.example: An agent asked to prepare a compliance filing, working through evidence collection, gap analysis, and drafting across several days without being re-briefed.
terms.definition: An agent breaking a long-running objective into a sequence of sub-goals, where each completed step sets the context for the next, so work continues across many cycles without a human restating the aim. It is what makes long-horizon autonomy possible, and it is also where drift begins, because an error early in the chain is inherited by every step after it and rarely re-examined.

terms.example: Building a product taxonomy so a retrieval system can answer questions the raw documents never state directly.
terms.definition: The practice of turning what an organisation knows into structures a machine can use: ontologies, taxonomies, rules, and curated knowledge bases. It predates modern AI and has returned to relevance because retrieval systems are only as good as the structure beneath them, and because a knowledge base can be corrected in one place and audited, where a model's learned behaviour cannot.

terms.example: Rejecting a generated database query that does not parse or touches a table outside the agent's scope, before it reaches the database.
terms.definition: Checking a model or agent's output against rules, a schema, or a second system before it is acted on or shown, so that a wrong answer does not become a wrong action. It is a control point rather than an accuracy technique: validation does not make the model better, it makes the failure visible while it can still be caught, which is why it belongs on the path between generation and execution rather than in evaluation.

terms.example: An assistant recalling a user's preferred report format from earlier sessions, held in a profile store that a deletion request must also reach.
terms.definition: Adapting a system's output to an individual using their history, preferences, or context. In AI systems this usually means retrieval over stored user data rather than a separate model for each person, which is why it sits inside privacy scope rather than beside it: the personalization store is a record about the user, subject to retention schedules, access controls, and erasure requests like any other.

terms.example: An agent finding a required document missing and constructing a new route to the same objective instead of failing the run.
terms.definition: An agent revising or discarding its current plan after the world fails to match its expectations, rather than continuing to execute steps that no longer apply. Replanning is much of what separates an agent from a script, and it is also where cost and loop risk enter, because an agent that may replan without limit can pursue a goal indefinitely and bill for every attempt.

terms.origin: Released as an open-source Python library in October 2022 by Harrison Chase; a JavaScript version followed.
terms.example: A support application that uses LangChain to retrieve relevant policy documents, pass them to a model, and call a ticketing tool if the model decides a ticket is needed.
terms.definition: An open-source framework for building applications that call language models, providing prebuilt pieces for chaining model calls, connecting tools, loading documents, and running agents. It is the orchestration layer: it decides what gets called in what order, rather than supplying the model or the data.

lenses.body: You hand LlamaIndex documents and it gives you a query engine. The pieces it owns are the ones you would otherwise write yourself: loaders for the file formats your data actually arrives in, a chunking step, an index over the chunks, a retriever, and a response synthesiser that assembles the retrieved passages into a prompt. The value is in the connectors and the defaults rather than in any single idea, which is why teams reach for it when the hard part is ingestion rather than orchestration.

Retrieval-augmented generation has two halves: find the right passage, then write an answer from it. LlamaIndex is a framework for the first half and a thin wrapper over the second. Studying it is a good way to see that the interesting engineering in a question-answering system is almost entirely in how documents are split, indexed and ranked, and almost never in the call to the model.

LlamaIndex is one of two or three obvious choices for building a system that answers questions from your own documents rather than from what a model memorised. Choosing it is a low-stakes decision: it is open source, the abstractions are shallow, and the work that survives a change of framework, cleaning the documents and deciding what good retrieval means, is the work that costs money either way. Ask what the team plans to do about evaluation before asking which framework they picked.

If you want a chatbot that answers from your own handbook, contracts or product data rather than making things up, this is one of the tools a developer would use to build it. You would not install it yourself. What is worth knowing is that the quality of that assistant depends far more on how tidy and well organised your documents are than on which tool is used to read them.

terms.origin: Started as GPT Index in late 2022 by Jerry Liu, renamed LlamaIndex in 2023.
terms.example: Indexing a company handbook so an assistant answers policy questions from the handbook text rather than from model memory.
terms.definition: An open-source framework focused on connecting language models to private data: loading documents, splitting and indexing them, retrieving the relevant pieces, and feeding them to a model. It overlaps with LangChain but is generally simpler for retrieval-heavy applications and broader for document ingestion.

lenses.body: Semantic Kernel puts a model behind the same dependency-injection and plugin conventions a .NET service already uses. You register existing methods as plugins, the kernel exposes them to the model as callable functions, and the orchestration layer decides which to invoke. For a team whose codebase is C# and whose services already exist, that is a shorter path than reimplementing the integration in Python.

Its distinguishing feature was never capability, it was language. Most model orchestration frameworks are Python first, and a large share of enterprise line-of-business code is not Python. Semantic Kernel let .NET and Java shops add model features without standing up a second stack in a second language. Microsoft has since converged this lineage with AutoGen into the Agent Framework, so treat the framework choice as a five-year decision and read the migration path before committing.

The security question with any plugin architecture is what the model is permitted to call and with whose credentials. A registered plugin is a real function against a real system, so prompt injection in a retrieved document becomes an attempted invocation of that function. Review which plugins are registered, what identity each runs under, and whether any of them write rather than read, before reviewing the model.

Look at Semantic Kernel to see the plugin pattern clearly. A model on its own can only produce text; it becomes useful by being given a set of functions it may call and a loop that executes the calls and feeds back the results. The kernel is that loop. Almost every agent framework is a variation on it, so the pattern is worth learning once and recognising everywhere.

terms.origin: Released by Microsoft in March 2023 with C# and .NET as the primary path; Python and Java followed. Entered maintenance mode in April 2026 when Microsoft shipped Agent Framework 1.0 as its successor.
terms.example: A .NET line-of-business application registering its existing invoice-lookup service as a plugin so a model can call it during a conversation.
terms.definition: Microsoft's open-source orchestration SDK for adding language models to conventional applications through plugins, connectors, memory, and agents. Its distinguishing feature is first-class .NET and Java support, which most competing frameworks lack.

terms.origin: Announced in public preview October 2025, reached Release Candidate February 2026, and shipped version 1.0 on 3 April 2026.
terms.example: Composing a copywriter agent and a reviewer agent into a sequential workflow where each hands its output to the next.
terms.definition: Microsoft's unified agent SDK, built by the same teams as Semantic Kernel and AutoGen and positioned as the successor to both. It combines AutoGen's agent abstractions with Semantic Kernel's enterprise features and adds graph-based workflows for multi-agent orchestration, with native Model Context Protocol and Agent-to-Agent support.

terms.origin: Grew out of the Demonstrate-Search-Predict work at Stanford NLP (research beginning 2022); the DSPy paper was published in October 2023. Name is a backronym for Declarative Self-improving Python.
terms.example: Compiling a classification pipeline against fifty labelled examples so the optimizer finds the instructions and demonstrations that score highest, instead of hand-editing a prompt.
terms.definition: A framework that treats prompting as an optimization problem rather than a writing task. You declare inputs and outputs as a signature, compose modules, supply a metric and example data, and an optimizer compiles the best-scoring prompts and few-shot examples. Changing models means recompiling rather than rewriting.

terms.origin: Representational State Transfer was defined in Roy Fielding's 2000 doctoral dissertation.
terms.example: Posting a JSON body containing a prompt to a provider's completions endpoint and reading the generated text from the JSON response.
terms.definition: An interface style where a client calls a service over HTTP using standard methods against addressable resources, usually exchanging JSON. It is the default way applications talk to AI model providers: nearly every hosted model is reached through a REST endpoint.

terms.origin: Released by Google as open source in 2015, built on HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.
terms.example: A model-serving runtime exposing a gRPC endpoint that an internal service calls for low-latency inference, while the public-facing API stays REST.
terms.definition: A remote procedure call framework that uses a binary serialization format and a defined service contract instead of JSON over HTTP verbs. In AI systems it is common between internal services and for model-serving runtimes, where its lower overhead and native streaming matter more than the human readability REST offers.

terms.example: Choosing direct REST calls for a single-purpose feature, and an orchestration framework only once several models, tools, and retrieval steps must be coordinated.
terms.definition: The recurring ways applications connect to models: calling a provider REST API directly, going through an orchestration framework such as LangChain or Semantic Kernel, exposing capabilities to the model as callable tools via function calling, standardising those tools behind the Model Context Protocol, or serving models internally over gRPC. The choice sets what has to be audited, since each pattern puts the boundary between application logic and model decision in a different place.

terms.origin: Formed in 2019 from the merger of the OpenTracing and OpenCensus projects; a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
terms.example: An agent emitting OTel spans for each model call and tool invocation, routed to a self-hosted collector today and a hosted platform tomorrow with no code change.
terms.definition: The vendor-neutral standard for emitting traces, metrics, and logs from software. AI observability tools have converged on it, which means an application instrumented once can send its telemetry to any compatible backend. Instrumenting with OpenTelemetry rather than a vendor SDK is what makes switching observability vendors a configuration change instead of a re-instrumentation project.

terms.example: A single agent run producing one parent span and forty child spans covering model calls, retrievals, and tool executions.
terms.definition: One timed unit of work inside a trace: a single model call, a retrieval step, a tool invocation. Spans nest, so a parent span for an agent run contains child spans for each step it took. Span count is what most observability vendors bill on, and a long agent run can emit thousands, which is why span-based pricing behaves very differently for agents than for chatbots.

terms.example: Opening one trace to find that an agent called the search tool three times, got empty results twice, and answered from its own assumption.
terms.definition: Following one request across every service and step it touches, assembled into a single timeline. For multi-step AI applications this is the difference between knowing an answer was wrong and knowing which retrieval returned the wrong document, which tool failed, and how long each step took. Logs tell you a run finished; a trace tells you what it did.

terms.origin: Developed by Arize AI as a set of OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for LLM applications.
terms.example: Instrumenting a RAG pipeline with OpenInference so any compatible platform can show the retrieved documents as retrieval spans rather than opaque function calls.
terms.definition: A convention layer on top of OpenTelemetry that defines how to describe AI-specific work in a span: what counts as a prompt, a completion, a retrieval, a tool call, token counts. OpenTelemetry says how to emit a span; OpenInference says what the fields inside an LLM span should mean, so different tools read the same trace the same way.

terms.example: Average prompt length creeping up over a month as a retrieval step returns steadily longer chunks, doubling per-request cost with no code change.
terms.definition: A gradual change over time in how many tokens a workload consumes per request, without an intended change to the application. Causes include growing context or history, prompt edits that add examples, retrieval returning longer passages, or a provider changing default behaviour. It matters because cost scales with tokens, so drift shows up as a rising bill before it shows up as a bug.

terms.example: Routing all model traffic through a gateway so cost limits and provider failover are enforced centrally rather than reimplemented in every service.
terms.definition: A service that sits between an application and model providers, handling routing, failover, caching, rate limiting, key management, and usage logging in one place. The trade is architectural: a gateway gives central control and near-zero integration effort, but it sits in the request path, so its availability becomes your availability. SDK-based observability logs alongside your code instead, failing to telemetry loss rather than request failure.

terms.origin: Popularised as a named metric by the Ragas framework (Es et al., 2024); TruLens calls the equivalent measure groundedness.
terms.example: An answer making four claims where three trace to the retrieved documents and one does not scores 0.75.
terms.definition: Whether every claim in an answer is supported by the retrieved context, scored by breaking the answer into individual claims and checking each one against the source. Usually reported 0 to 1 as the fraction of supported claims. It is the direct hallucination measure for a RAG system, and it is reference-free: no human-written gold answer is needed, so it can run on live production traffic.

terms.origin: One of the core Ragas metrics; TruLens carries an equivalent feedback function.
terms.example: Asking for a filing deadline and receiving an accurate but rambling summary of the whole statute: high faithfulness, low answer relevance.
terms.definition: Whether the answer actually addresses the question asked, independent of whether it is true. A response can be perfectly faithful to its sources and still evade the question, or bury the answer in unrequested detail. Typically scored by generating candidate questions from the answer and measuring how closely they match the original.

terms.origin: A core Ragas retrieval metric.
terms.example: Retrieving ten chunks of which three bear on the question, with the best one ranked eighth, scores poorly on precision even if the final answer happens to be right.
terms.definition: What proportion of the retrieved chunks are actually relevant to the question, and whether the relevant ones ranked highly. It measures the retriever, not the model. Low precision means the generator is working through noise, which both raises cost and increases the chance it latches onto an irrelevant passage.

terms.origin: A core Ragas retrieval metric.
terms.example: A legal answer scoring high on faithfulness while context recall sits at 0.62 because the retriever consistently missed the second governing statute.
terms.definition: Whether retrieval fetched everything needed to answer the question. Unlike faithfulness and answer relevance it generally requires ground truth, since something must define what should have been retrieved. It catches the failure the other metrics miss: a confident, well-grounded answer built on half the evidence.

terms.origin: Named by TruLens as a three-part evaluation pattern.
terms.example: Context relevance falling while groundedness holds steady points at the retriever, not the prompt.
terms.definition: Evaluating a retrieval system along three axes at once: is the retrieved context relevant to the question, is the answer grounded in that context, and does the answer address the question. Scoring all three localises a failure to retrieval or generation instead of only recording that output quality dropped.

terms.example: Running faithfulness and answer relevance on production traffic nightly, while a smaller labelled golden set carries the reference-based metrics.
terms.definition: Scoring an output without a human-written correct answer to compare against, using the question and retrieved context as the standard instead. It is what makes evaluation affordable at scale and possible on live traffic, since writing gold answers for thousands of queries is not. The trade is that it measures internal consistency, not truth: a system can score well while the underlying knowledge base is stale or wrong.

terms.example: A pytest suite failing the build if any response omits its citation field, before faithfulness is scored at all.
terms.definition: Checks with one correct answer that do not involve a model judging anything: valid JSON, required field present, cited source appears in the retrieved set, no PII in output, latency under a threshold, refusal on a prohibited prompt. They are cheap, instant, and repeatable, and they belong in CI as hard gates before any model-graded metric runs. Model-graded scores tell you how good an answer is; assertions tell you whether it is even shaped correctly.

terms.example: A ministry reporting national intelligent computing capacity in the low thousands of EFLOPS, without naming the precision the figure was measured at.
terms.definition: One quintillion floating point operations per second, 10^18, the unit used to size supercomputers and national compute fleets. It sits above petaFLOPS at 10^15 and below zettaFLOPS at 10^21. Read any headline figure carefully, because the precision is rarely stated: exascale in high performance computing means FP64, while national AI capacity totals are usually quoted at the lower precisions used for AI work such as FP16 or INT8, so the two numbers are not comparable even though both are printed as EFLOPS.

terms.origin: Standard industry term that became common with the growth of internet exchange points in the 1990s.
terms.example: A growing online retailer might use colocation to keep its servers in a professionally managed facility near major internet hubs, avoiding the cost of constructing its own data center.
terms.definition: Colocation is a data center service where a business rents space, power, cooling, and network connectivity for its own servers and IT equipment inside a facility owned and operated by a third party. Instead of building a private data center, the customer places its hardware in a shared building alongside other companies' equipment.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: The operator reported that the facility supports 4.7 megawatts of critical IT load, leaving about 2 megawatts available for new customers.
terms.definition: Critical IT load is the amount of electrical power that a data center's computing equipment, such as servers, storage systems, and network devices, needs to operate. It does not include power used for cooling, lighting, or other building systems.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term, combining hyper meaning beyond normal with scaler for scaling up computing resources.
terms.example: When a hyperscaler has an outage, apps and websites that depend on its cloud can stop working for millions of users.
terms.definition: A hyperscaler is a company that builds and runs very large networks of data centers to provide computing power and online services at massive scale, such as Amazon Web Services, Google, or Meta.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term used in data centre engineering.
terms.example: A data centre with N+1 cooling redundancy has enough extra air conditioners that one can break and the servers still stay cool.
terms.definition: N+1 redundancy means a system has one more backup unit than the minimum needed to run. If any single unit fails, the extra one takes over so service continues without interruption.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term combining the electrical unit gigawatt with the idea of a multi building data centre campus.
terms.example: OpenAI is expanding Stargate to Michigan with a new one gigawatt campus that strengthens America's AI infrastructure.
terms.definition: A gigawatt campus is a data centre site designed to use one gigawatt of electricity, which is one billion watts or one thousand megawatts. It describes a very large cluster of buildings built together to run AI and cloud computing at massive scale.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A data centre operator paid part of the cost of a new 180 megawatt substation so the local utility could handle the extra load.
terms.definition: A substation is a facility that receives high power electricity from the grid and adjusts it to a level that buildings like data centres can safely use. It also helps route power from different sources so a site keeps running if one supply fails.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: An insurer pricing supply chain cover for a new data centre must account for transformer lead times that can run to four years.
terms.definition: A transformer is a piece of electrical equipment that changes the voltage of electricity, stepping it up or down so power can move safely and efficiently. In data centres, transformers take high voltage power from the grid and reduce it to the lower voltages that servers and cooling systems need.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: The operator page lists 130,000 square feet of data halls for customer server racks.
terms.definition: A data hall is a large room or area inside a data center building where servers and other IT equipment are kept. It usually has a raised floor and special cooling to keep the equipment from overheating.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The Uptime Institute introduced the tier system in the 1990s to give data centre owners a common way to describe reliability.
terms.example: An AI company that cannot afford any downtime for its training runs will often choose a Tier IV data centre over a Tier III one.
terms.definition: Tier III and Tier IV are the two highest levels in a four level rating system created by the Uptime Institute to grade how reliable a data centre is. A Tier III centre can be maintained or repaired without turning off the computers, while a Tier IV centre can keep running even if one major piece of equipment fails completely.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The Green Grid, an industry consortium, introduced PUE in 2007 as a standard way to compare data centre energy efficiency.
terms.example: A data centre with a PUE of 1.4 uses 1.4 watts of total building power for every 1 watt that reaches the servers.
terms.definition: PUE, or Power Usage Effectiveness, is a number that shows how efficiently a data centre uses electricity. It compares the total power a whole building uses with the power that actually reaches the computers and servers. A lower number is better, with 1.0 meaning all power goes to the computers and none is wasted on cooling or other overhead.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: If a chiller breaks down during a heat wave, the data centre may lose cooling and servers could shut down.
terms.definition: A chiller is a large machine that cools water or another liquid, which is then circulated through a data centre to remove heat from servers and other equipment. It is part of the cooling system that keeps computers from overheating.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: At the typical 40 kW per rack density used for AI training, a 30 MW facility could hold roughly 750 racks.
terms.definition: Rack density is how much electrical power one rack of servers uses, measured in kilowatts. A higher rack density means more computing power is packed into the same physical space.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A subsea cable cut can interrupt internet traffic between continents and lead to business interruption insurance claims.
terms.definition: A subsea cable is a cable laid on the ocean floor that carries data and communications between land locations, often across seas or oceans. It is a key part of the physical internet infrastructure.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A data center with GPU racks above 100 kW may switch to liquid cooling, and insurers then worry about the risk of leaks damaging the building.
terms.definition: Liquid cooling is a way to remove heat from computer equipment in a data center by running a liquid, such as water or a special fluid, close to or through the hot parts instead of blowing air over them. It is used because dense racks of AI chips produce too much heat for ordinary fans to handle.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term became common as data centre chips grew hotter and air cooling could not keep up.
terms.example: A data centre using direct to chip cooling runs coolant lines right up to each server's processors, so a leak could damage nearby electrical parts.
terms.definition: Direct to chip cooling is a way to cool data centre computers by running liquid coolant straight to the processors inside each server rack. The fluid sits very close to powered electrical parts, which removes heat more efficiently than air cooling but also creates a leak risk.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term.
terms.example: A data centre switched part of its site to immersion cooling to make the facility quieter and handle high density racks.
terms.definition: Immersion cooling is a way to cool computer equipment by placing the hardware directly into a special liquid that absorbs heat, instead of using fans and air.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: The coolant distribution unit uses ultrasonic flow meters and pressure sensors to detect a leak and close its isolation valves before much fluid escapes.
terms.definition: A piece of equipment in a data centre that moves cooling liquid to the computer racks and back, while watching the flow and pressure of that liquid. It can also shut off the liquid supply automatically if something goes wrong.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A data centre operator signed a power purchase agreement with a wind farm to lock in electricity costs for ten years.
terms.definition: A power purchase agreement is a long term contract in which a data centre or another large energy user agrees to buy electricity from a generator or utility at a set price. It helps secure a stable power supply and can support renewable energy projects. If the seller fails to deliver, the buyer may face higher costs or power shortages.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term used by electric utilities and grid planners.
terms.example: A data centre project can be delayed for years if its position in the interconnection queue is far back.
terms.definition: The interconnection queue is the waiting list kept by the company that runs the electricity network. New large electricity users, like AI data centres, must join this list and wait for approval before they can connect to the grid and receive power.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A data centre in Michigan uses free cooling to take advantage of the cold winter air and reduce how much its mechanical cooling system has to run.
terms.definition: Free cooling is a way to cool a data centre by using cold outside air or water instead of running power hungry air conditioning machines. It works best in places with cold seasons, where the outside temperature can do most of the cooling work.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Fuel cells were invented in the 19th century, but their use as on site power for data centres is a recent development driven by grid constraints.
terms.example: AEP Ohio proposed a 228 cell, six acre fuel cell installation to power the Scioto Darby data centre campus until new transmission capacity was ready.
terms.definition: A fuel cell is a device that makes electricity by combining a fuel, usually natural gas, with oxygen in a chemical reaction, without burning it. In data centres, fuel cells are installed on site to provide power, often as a temporary bridge source while waiting for new transmission lines.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The phrase comes from utility metering, where anything on the customer's side of the electricity meter is behind the meter.
terms.example: A data center operator built a gas plant behind the meter so its servers could run without waiting years for a grid connection.
terms.definition: Behind the meter means electricity is generated on site or nearby and used directly by a facility, without passing through the public utility grid. The power is wired straight from the generator to the building, so it never crosses the customer's utility meter.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A startup uses a GPU cloud to train its language model for a few hours instead of building a server room.
terms.definition: A GPU cloud is a service that rents out access to powerful computer chips made for AI and machine learning over the internet, so companies can run heavy AI tasks without buying their own hardware.
