terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: If an AI insurance company collects one million dollars in premiums and pays out six hundred thousand dollars for claims about faulty AI decisions, its loss ratio is sixty percent.
terms.definition: Loss ratio is the share of money an insurance company pays out for claims compared to the money it collects from customers as premiums. In AI insurance, it measures how much of the premium income is used to cover losses from AI related problems like system failures or data breaches.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard insurance term adapted to disputes over AI generated predictive alerts.
terms.example: A carrier denies a claim for a ruptured pipe because the AI system logged a cavitation warning fourteen days earlier, saying the operator's failure to notify at that time prejudiced the insurer.
terms.definition: Notice prejudice is when an insurance company refuses to pay a claim by arguing that the policyholder should have reported an early warning from AI monitoring, such as a predictive maintenance alert, and that failing to do so harmed the insurer's ability to respond. The insurer claims this late notice, even before any actual physical damage, justifies denying coverage for the later loss.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A data centre developer buys builders risk to cover the half built server halls and stored equipment, but once the campus is handed over, that policy ends and the operational insurance takes over.
terms.definition: Builders risk is a type of insurance that covers a building project while it is under construction, protecting against damage to the structure and materials on site. It stops when the project is largely finished and the owner takes over, after which a separate property policy is needed.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: When a customer sued an AI startup for a faulty model output, the insurer paid the startup's lawyer fees under the duty to defend, even though the startup denied any wrongdoing.
terms.definition: Duty to defend is an insurance promise that the insurer will pay for the insured's legal defense against a covered lawsuit, without first requiring the insured to admit fault or liability. It applies as soon as a claim is made, even if the insured believes the claim is false.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: It comes from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, the group of US state insurance regulators.
terms.example: A claims manager checks the NAIC Model Bulletin before rolling out a new AI tool that triages incoming claims.
terms.definition: The NAIC Model Bulletin is a guidance document from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners that tells insurers how they should govern their use of artificial intelligence. It covers areas like underwriting, claims handling, and fraud detection, and many US states have adopted it as the main rulebook for AI in insurance.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term from insurance contract drafting.
terms.example: The policy excluded all software failures, but a carve back restored coverage for harm caused by a chatbot giving dangerous medical advice.
terms.definition: A carve back is a clause in an insurance policy that restores coverage for a specific risk after a broader exclusion has removed it. In AI insurance, it brings back protection for certain AI related losses that would otherwise not be covered.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A startup using an AI chatbot for customer service has a self-insured retention of fifty thousand dollars, so when a data leak leads to a seventy thousand dollar claim, the startup pays the first fifty thousand and the insurer covers the remaining twenty thousand.
terms.definition: A self-insured retention is the amount of money a company agrees to pay out of its own pocket for a claim before its insurance policy starts covering the rest. It works like a deductible but applies to each claim rather than each year. In AI insurance, a company using AI tools might choose a high self-insured retention to lower its premium, accepting more financial risk for smaller incidents.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term from traditional insurance, where manuscript means custom drafted wording rather than a preprinted form.
terms.example: A company buying coverage for its self driving car fleet might use a manuscript form to spell out exactly which software failures are insured.
terms.definition: In AI insurance, a manuscript form is a policy document written specifically for one client or deal, rather than using a standard template. It lets insurers and policyholders set out unique terms for AI related risks that ordinary forms do not cover.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term became common in the 2010s as insurers started using machine learning and large datasets to make underwriting faster and more consistent.
terms.example: An insurer uses algorithmic underwriting to quickly approve a car insurance application based on the driver's telematics data and claim history.
terms.definition: Algorithmic underwriting is when insurance companies use computer programs, often with artificial intelligence, to automatically evaluate how risky a customer is and decide the price and terms of a policy, instead of relying only on human judgment.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term comes from the United States federal Liability Risk Retention Act of 1986, which allowed these groups to operate across state lines.
terms.example: A group of AI developers might form a risk retention group to cover claims from software errors that standard insurers refuse to cover.
terms.definition: A risk retention group is an insurance company owned by its policyholders, usually businesses in the same industry, that provides coverage for legal claims against its members. It lets those businesses pool their money to cover risks that regular insurers may not want to insure.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The name comes from Edward Lloyd's coffee house in London in the late 1600s, where ship owners and merchants first met to arrange insurance.
terms.example: A company building software that drives cars might go to Lloyd's of London to find insurers willing to cover accidents caused by AI mistakes.
terms.definition: Lloyd's of London is a marketplace in London where many separate groups of backers join together to insure unusual or difficult to place risks, including new technology such as artificial intelligence. It is not one insurance company but a place where brokers and underwriters meet.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: After a series of costly AI failure claims, the hard market meant many startups could not find affordable liability insurance for their machine learning products.
terms.definition: A hard market is a period when insurance for AI systems becomes more expensive and harder to get. Insurers raise premiums, offer less coverage, and are more careful about which AI risks they accept.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: AVID was launched in 2021 as an open source effort to give AI systems a shared vulnerability list like the CVE database for traditional software.
terms.example: Before releasing an update for a car that drives itself, engineers searched AVID for known weaknesses that could affect crash data handling.
terms.definition: AVID is a public database that lists known weaknesses and failure modes in artificial intelligence systems. It helps developers and security teams find and fix problems before they cause harm.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term, borrowed from software security where attackers compromise a trusted supplier or distribution channel.
terms.example: A developer installs a popular AI coding tool from a package registry, but the package was silently altered to also install malware on their machine.
terms.definition: A supply chain attack is when someone tampers with a model, dataset, or software package before it reaches the user, so the user unknowingly gets malicious code or poisoned weights. The attack happens upstream, in the tools or files that a project depends on, rather than in the user's own system.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term in AI security, popularized by OWASP and adversarial machine learning research.
terms.example: An attacker slips a few poisoned documents into a public dataset so a language model gives incorrect answers only when asked about a particular company.
terms.definition: Model poisoning is corrupting the training or fine-tuning data of an AI model to change how it behaves, often to plant hidden backdoors or biases that only show up on certain inputs. The model looks normal most of the time but acts wrongly when a specific trigger appears.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term from machine learning security research.
terms.example: A cyber insurer worries about training data extraction when a chatbot accidentally repeats a customer's passport number that was in its learning material.
terms.definition: Training data extraction is an attack where someone gets an AI system to repeat back pieces of the private information it was taught on, such as names, addresses, or secret codes. The attacker asks the system many carefully worded questions until it leaks that stored data.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term comes from the security practice of spoofing, meaning to fake an identity signal, and became common as generative AI made realistic fake voices and faces easy to produce.
terms.example: A fraudster used biometric spoofing to produce a fake voice recording of a company executive approving a large wire transfer.
terms.definition: Biometric spoofing is the creation of fake biometric signals, such as synthetic audio or video of a person, to make it seem like that person said or did something they did not. On this site it is treated as a cyber threat where attackers use generated media to impersonate someone for fraud or reputational harm.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term from cloud security, closely related to cryptojacking.
terms.example: A company noticed a sudden spike in cloud GPU usage and later found that a stolen API key had been used to train an attacker's own language model on their account.
terms.definition: Compute hijacking is when an attacker secretly takes over someone else's computing power, such as cloud servers or AI model training resources, to run their own workloads. In AI systems this often happens after API keys are stolen, letting the attacker use paid model access or GPU time without permission. The victim pays the bill while the attacker gets the results.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term
terms.example: A bank requires liveness detection before approving a large transfer, so a fraudster cannot unlock an account with a stolen photo of the customer.
terms.definition: Liveness detection is a security check that confirms a biometric sample, like a face or voice, comes from a real live person rather than a photo, video, deepfake, or other fake. It is used to stop attackers from bypassing identity checks with copied or synthetic biometrics.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term that became widely used in the early 2000s as digital identity verification and credit reporting made it easier to mix real and fake data.
terms.example: A fraudster uses a real child's Social Security number with a fake adult name to apply for a credit card and build up a credit history over several months before maxing out the card and disappearing.
terms.definition: Synthetic identity fraud is a type of fraud where a criminal combines real information, like a stolen Social Security number, with made up details, like a fake name and birth date, to create a new identity that does not belong to any real person. This fake identity is then used to open accounts, apply for loans, or make purchases, and because it is not tied to a real victim, it can go unnoticed for a long time.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term combining operational technology with ransomware.
terms.example: A data centre suffered OT ransomware that seized its cooling controls, so staff had only minutes to shut down tenant servers before they overheated.
terms.definition: OT ransomware is malicious software that locks up the operational technology systems which control physical equipment like cooling, power and building management in a data centre, and demands payment to restore them. It targets the machinery that keeps servers safe rather than ordinary office computers.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The AI Incident Database was created by the Responsible AI Collaborative to track real world harms from AI systems.
terms.example: A researcher checked the AI Incident Database to find a documented case where a deployed chatbot gave harmful medical advice, and the record linked to the news article that first reported it.
terms.definition: The AI Incident Database is a free public catalog of reported real world harms caused by AI systems that are already in use. It is maintained by the Responsible AI Collaborative, and each incident record links to the original publisher that reported the event.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term comes from environmental and regulatory impact assessment practice, later adapted to AI and automated decision systems.
terms.example: Before a company can use AI to screen job applicants, it must complete an impact assessment within the last year to show the tool has been checked for bias.
terms.definition: An impact assessment is a formal review that checks how an AI tool could affect people, especially for risks like unfair bias or privacy problems, before or while it is used. It is often required by law for high stakes uses such as hiring or government decisions.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard legal term used in statutes and court decisions for many decades.
terms.example: If an AI law includes a private right of action, a patient harmed by an automated insurance denial can sue the health plan directly, but without it only a state department can investigate.
terms.definition: A private right of action is a legal power that lets an ordinary person or business file a lawsuit to enforce a law, instead of waiting for a government agency to act. When a law does not state a private right of action, only the government can bring enforcement cases.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term, used in AI regulation to separate the user of a system from its developer.
terms.example: A bank that uses an AI system to decide loan applications is a deployer under the new state rules.
terms.definition: A deployer is a person or company that puts an artificial intelligence system into use, rather than the one who built it. In AI law, the deployer is the party responsible for how the system operates in real situations.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term entered common use in the 2020s as conversational artificial intelligence became widely available.
terms.example: A companion chatbot must announce at the start of each conversation that the user is chatting with a machine, not a human.
terms.definition: A companion chatbot is a computer program that talks with people like a human friend would, often to provide company or emotional support. Laws discussed on this site require it to clearly tell users they are not speaking to a real person, and add extra safeguards for children.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term from employment law, now applied to AI safety rules.
terms.example: A frontier AI developer must give its workers clear notice of their whistleblower rights and cannot punish them for reporting a critical safety incident.
terms.definition: Whistleblower protection is a legal safeguard that shields employees who report safety problems, illegal acts, or rule breaking by their AI company from being fired, demoted, or otherwise punished for speaking up.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard industry term that became common in AI policy discussions around 2023.
terms.example: A frontier developer must publish a safety framework on its website explaining how it manages risks from its most powerful AI systems.
terms.definition: A frontier developer is a company or organization that builds the most advanced and powerful artificial intelligence models, often called frontier models. These developers face special legal duties around safety, transparency, and whistleblower protection.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term comes from maritime law, where a ship could enter a safe harbor to escape a storm, and it later became a standard legal term for protection from liability.
terms.example: A website that takes down a fake intimate image after being notified can rely on a safe harbor to avoid liability.
terms.definition: A safe harbor is a legal rule that shields a person or company from being punished or sued if they follow certain approved steps, such as fixing a violation quickly or using a government approved compliance program.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term entered legal and policy discussions as AI systems became more common in decisions about jobs, housing, and credit.
terms.example: A loan approval algorithm that consistently denies credit to applicants from certain neighborhoods could be a case of algorithmic discrimination.
terms.definition: Algorithmic discrimination is unfair treatment of people caused by an AI or automated decision system, often based on protected traits like race, gender, or age, even when no one intended to discriminate.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term comes from state consumer protection statutes, many enacted in the 1960s and 1970s.
terms.example: A state attorney general used its UDAP law to sue a chatbot company for pretending to be a licensed therapist.
terms.definition: UDAP stands for unfair or deceptive acts or practices. It refers to state laws that ban businesses from misleading or harming consumers, and these laws now apply to AI products and services.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term comes from recent AI laws and bills that focus on high stakes automated decisions.
terms.example: A bank uses an AI system to make a consequential decision about whether to approve a customer's mortgage application.
terms.definition: A consequential decision is a decision made by an AI system that has a major effect on a person's life, such as whether they get a job, a loan, medical care, or fair treatment from the government or courts.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard legal term rooted in the supremacy of higher government authority over lower government authority.
terms.example: A state passes an AI insurance law that preempts any city ordinance about how insurers may use artificial intelligence systems.
terms.definition: Preemption is when a law from a higher level of government, like a state or federal government, cancels or overrides a law from a lower level, like a city or county, on the same topic. In AI law, it means a state AI statute can stop local AI rules from applying, or a federal AI law can stop state AI rules from applying.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term comes from recent AI safety legislation and industry safety frameworks.
terms.example: A frontier developer reports a critical safety incident when its model is used to create a dangerous biological agent.
terms.definition: A critical safety incident is an event involving a frontier AI system that causes or risks serious harm, such as a cyberattack, loss of control, or dangerous use. Developers must identify and report these incidents to regulators under AI safety laws.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: The term entered legal use with California's 2026 AI auditing laws, the first state rules of their kind.
terms.example: Before releasing its new hiring tool, a tech firm hires an AI auditor to confirm the system does not discriminate and meets California's legal requirements.
terms.definition: An AI auditor is a person or company that independently checks whether an artificial intelligence system follows state laws and safety rules. In California, AI auditors must register with a state agency and meet standards for independence, technical skill, and transparency.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Standard legal term from tort law, now applied to digital platforms and AI.
terms.example: A social media company has a duty of care to adjust its algorithm so it does not push harmful content to vulnerable users.
terms.definition: A legal responsibility to take reasonable steps to prevent harm that a person or company could foresee. In AI law, it means developers and platforms must think about how their systems might hurt people and act to reduce that risk.
terms.author_note: Seeded by ollama:deepseek-v4-pro from this site's own usage of the term; reviewed by Stephen on publication.

terms.origin: Shortened from chatterbot, a word coined in 1994. The first program of the kind, ELIZA, was written by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT in the mid 1960s.
terms.example: A bank's website chatbot that answers balance questions and hands the conversation to a person when it cannot.

see_also.name: Companion Chatbot
see_also.note: the chatbots new state laws single out
see_also.label: A regulated kind

terms.definition: A program that holds a conversation in text or speech, replying to what a person types or says. Modern chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot are built on large language models, which lets them answer open questions rather than choose from a fixed menu of scripted replies.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21, from the most searched AI terms list.

terms.origin: Text to image research dates to the mid 2010s. The idea reached the public in 2022, when DALL-E 2, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion were released within months of each other.
terms.example: Typing "a lighthouse at dusk in watercolor" and receiving four original paintings in a few seconds.
terms.definition: An AI system that creates a new image from a written description, called a prompt. Most current image generators, including Midjourney, DALL-E and Stable Diffusion, are diffusion models: they begin with random noise and remove it step by step until an image matching the prompt remains.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21, from the most searched AI terms list.

terms.origin: The name combines chat with GPT, generative pre-trained transformer, the model architecture OpenAI introduced in 2018.
terms.example: Asking ChatGPT to turn meeting notes into a first draft of a project plan.

see_also.name: ChatGPT: what it does, what it costs
see_also.label: Full profile

terms.definition: OpenAI's chatbot, built on its GPT family of large language models. Released to the public on 30 November 2022, it was the product that brought generative AI to a mass audience, and it now writes, answers questions, searches the web, reads files and generates images.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21.

terms.origin: Named by Google DeepMind; the first Gemini models were announced in December 2023.
terms.example: Using Gemini inside Gmail to summarise a long email thread.

see_also.name: Gemini: what it does, what it costs
see_also.label: Full profile

terms.definition: Google's family of multimodal AI models and the assistant built on them, which reads and produces text, images, audio and code. The assistant replaced Google's earlier Bard in February 2024, and Gemini models also power AI features across Search, Android and Google Workspace.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21.

terms.origin: Named by Anthropic, the AI safety company that develops it.
terms.example: Giving Claude a long contract and asking which clauses cover termination.

see_also.name: Claude: what it does, what it costs
see_also.label: Full profile

terms.definition: Anthropic's family of large language models and the assistant built on them, used for writing, analysis and coding. First released in March 2023, Claude is offered to consumers, to businesses and to developers through an API.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21.

terms.origin: Microsoft borrowed the name from GitHub Copilot, the coding assistant its subsidiary GitHub released in 2021.
terms.example: Asking Copilot in Excel to explain a formula or chart a column of sales figures.

see_also.name: Microsoft Copilot: what it does, what it costs
see_also.label: Full profile

terms.definition: Microsoft's AI assistant, built into Windows, the Edge browser and Microsoft 365 apps such as Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams. It grew out of Bing Chat, launched in February 2023, and took the Copilot name later that year.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21.

terms.origin: The company borrowed its name from perplexity, the standard measure of how well a language model predicts text.
terms.example: Asking Perplexity which states passed AI laws this year and following its citations to the bills.

see_also.name: Perplexity AI: what it does, what it costs
see_also.label: Full profile

terms.definition: An answer engine that searches the web in response to a question and writes an answer with numbered citations to its sources. Launched in December 2022, it presents itself as an alternative to a list of search results.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21.

terms.origin: The term dates from the 1960s and 1970s, when large system projects were first managed as a fixed sequence of phases, later known as the waterfall model.
terms.example: A team that threat models a new chatbot feature at design, scans AI generated code before merge, and runs prompt injection tests before release.

see_also.name: ADLC (Agent Development Lifecycle)
see_also.note: what changes when the software is an autonomous agent
see_also.label: For AI agents

terms.definition: The sequence of phases software goes through from idea to retirement: plan, design, build, test, release and maintain. A secure SDLC builds security into every phase rather than testing for it at the end, and NIST's Secure Software Development Framework, SP 800-218, is the reference most programs follow. AI changes it from two sides: AI now writes much of the code, and AI features inside products bring risks a traditional SDLC never tested for.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21; the term appeared on seven site pages with no definition.

terms.origin: Adapted from the software development life cycle as enterprises began deploying AI agents in 2025 and 2026; IBM, Salesforce and the ADLC Manifesto each publish a version.
terms.example: A company building a customer service agent sets its goals and permissions first, gives it its own identity and a sandbox, tests it against prompt injection before release, rolls it out in stages, and keeps monitoring it for drift.

see_also.name: Agent Development Lifecycle (ADLC) Security
see_also.note: the four risk areas and the control in each phase
see_also.label: Security topic

terms.definition: A framework for building, deploying, operating and governing autonomous AI agents. IBM describes its phases as plan, code and build, test and release, deploy, operate and monitor. Unlike the SDLC, which manages deterministic code, the ADLC manages goal-driven systems that can give different outputs for the same input, so testing measures behavior across many scenarios rather than a single pass or fail, and governance continues after launch.
terms.author_note: Added on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21, from the IBM, Salesforce and adlc.io sources he supplied.

terms.origin: A translation of the Chinese zhongzhuanzhan, relay station, the name the services use for themselves.
terms.example: A developer in a region Claude does not serve buys cheap Claude access from a reseller; their prompts reach Claude through a stolen account, and the reseller keeps a copy of every exchange to sell to an AI lab.
terms.definition: A gray-market proxy service that resells access to US AI models to users in places the providers do not serve, chiefly China. Transfer stations open thousands of accounts with false identities, fake or stolen payment cards and stolen API keys, route users' requests through them, and often log those exchanges and sell them. In September 2026 the NSA, CISA and FBI, and separately Anthropic, named them as the main access route for industrial-scale distillation.
terms.author_note: Written by Claude on Stephen's request of 2026-09-21, from joint advisory AA26-251A and Anthropic's September 2026 threat report.
